title: Agentic RAG
text:
Retrieval inside the loop






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


Everything on the previous pages answers one question well: given a query, find passages and write. None of it decides whether to retrieve, what to ask for, or when to stop. Agentic RAG treats retrieval as an action the model can take, in a loop, rather than as a fixed first step.
That is the same turn already described on Compound AI systems and LLMs for agents: a workflow becomes more agent-like when the model writes the next step. The lecture’s three decisions are a useful test for any such loop.






Everyday example



A careful researcher does not always go to the library. Sometimes they already know the answer. Sometimes they need a different book from the one they first pulled, or a second search with a better keyword. And they need a rule for when to stop reading and start writing. Self-RAG is the habit of asking “do I need a source?” and of grading the page you found. CRAG is a critic who can send you back for a better search. Search-R1 is practice: you learn the habit by being rewarded for questions you eventually get right.







flowchart TD
  Q["Question"] --> D{{"Retrieve, or answer directly?"}}
  D -->|answer| A["Write the answer"]
  D -->|retrieve| S["Issue a search query"]
  S --> R["Read the result"]
  R --> G{{"Is this good enough?"}}
  G -->|yes| A
  G -->|no| S








Self-RAG
Self-RAG (Asai et al., ICLR 2024; the lecture writes 2024) trains a language model to retrieve on demand, to generate, and to critique its own uses of evidence. Special reflection tokens mark whether a retrieval was needed, whether a passage was relevant, and whether a claim is supported. Segments can be generated in parallel from different passages and then compared, so the model can prefer a supported span over an irrelevant one and, if need be, retrieve again.







Figure 1: Self-RAG retrieves on demand, generates from several passages, and critiques which segment is supported — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 57. Original: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection (Asai et al., 2024).




The point is not a new index. It is a model that has learned the three decisions — retrieve or not, which evidence to trust, whether to try again — instead of following a fixed retrieve-then-generate graph.


CRAG: a critic on the retrieval
Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (Yan, Jiang, Ren and colleagues, 2024) adds an explicit evaluator. A critic looks at the retrieved documents, grades them as correct, ambiguous, or incorrect, and triggers different actions: keep and refine the internal knowledge, or rewrite the query and search the web when the retrieval is wrong. The generator then sees a cleaned or replaced context, not whatever the first retriever happened to return.







Figure 2: CRAG’s critic grades the retrieved documents and branches: refine, or search again — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 58. Original: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (Yan et al., 2024).




If Self-RAG folds the critique into the generator, CRAG factors it out as a retrieval evaluator. Both are answers to the same failure: a pipeline that always trusts its first top-\(k\).


Search-R1: learning the search policy
Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) goes a step further: it learns a multi-turn search policy with reinforcement learning. The model thinks in a <think> block, issues a <search> query when it lacks knowledge, reads <information>, and may search again before it commits to an <answer>. The training setup the lecture shows is the one we already met for verifiable rewards — PPO, and GRPO — with the search engine in the loop and a reward for a correct final answer.







Figure 3: Search-R1 trains a policy that can call a search engine across several turns, with PPO or GRPO — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 60. Original: Search-R1: Training LLMs to Reason and Leverage Search Engines with Reinforcement Learning (Jin et al., 2025).




The example in the lecture is a comparison of two birth dates: the model searches, finds one person, searches again, and only then answers. That is retrieval as a skill, trained against a checkable outcome, not as a preprocessor.


In one table








System
Who decides to retrieve?
What happens if the evidence is weak?




Naive RAG
The pipeline, always, once
The generator sees it anyway


Self-RAG
The model, via reflection tokens
Critique, and another retrieve if needed


CRAG
A critic on the retrieved set
Refine, or rewrite and search again


Search-R1
A learned, multi-turn policy
Another <search>, until it can answer





FAQ
Is agentic RAG just “RAG plus an agent framework”? Not necessarily. The papers above change who decides and how that decision is trained. You can wrap naive RAG in a tool loop; Self-RAG, CRAG and Search-R1 are recipes for making the loop itself smarter.
Do I always want the model to retrieve? No. Some questions are already in the weights, and an extra passage can distract. A model that can skip retrieval is part of the point of Self-RAG.
How is this different from ordinary tool use? Search is a tool. What is new is the policy: when to call it, how to rewrite the query, how to grade the result, and when to stop. For the shape of a single tool call, see Compound AI systems. For the risk of a loop that never stops, or that trusts a poisoned passage, see failure modes.

title: Indexing for RAG
text:
Cutting the library into shelves






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


Retrieval is only as honest as the pieces you stored. If you cut a document in the wrong place, the best retriever in the world will still hand the model a fragment that does not mean what it should. Indexing is that unglamorous work: how you chunk, how you give a chunk its context, how you embed it, and how you organise the shelves so a query can find it quickly.






Everyday example



Think of photocopying a handbook into index cards. Cut too short and a card says “due Thursday” with no idea which Thursday. Cut too long and one card mixes grading, office hours, and the late-day policy, so its “topic” is a blur. Write a one-line header on each card — “From the grading section of the autumn syllabus” — and the same sentence becomes findable. That header is contextual retrieval. A tree of summary cards, or a map of who relates to whom, is what you reach for when the answer is not on a single card.




Embeddings, in one table
A retriever that uses vectors needs two things: a fixed-dimension representation of each chunk, and a similarity (usually cosine or an inner product). The lecture’s landscape is enough to steer by; we will not retell the history of word2vec here.



Type
Examples
One vector covers




Static word
word2vec, GloVe
a word type


Contextual
BERT, RoBERTa
a token in context


Passage
Sentence-BERT, DPR, E5
a chunk


Multimodal
CLIP
text or image, in a shared space


Graph
node2vec, GNN encoders
a node or a relation



Passage embeddings are the usual unit for RAG: one vector per chunk, compared to a query vector. How you cut the chunk matters as much as which encoder you pick.


Chunking
Fixed-size chunking cuts on a token budget, often in the 100–500 range. Too small, and the vector has no context. Too large, and one vector averages several topics. A 10–20% overlap is a common hedge, so a sentence is less likely to be split at the cut. Semantic or structure-aware chunking follows headings, sections, or sentences instead of a raw counter. You can also carry metadata or a short summary with each chunk, or ask a model to find natural breakpoints. The lecture points at a Databricks guide to chunking strategies for a practical tour.
The same short grading paragraph, split three ways, is the picture to keep:







Figure 1: The same syllabus paragraph, cut to a fixed size, cut with overlap, and split on structure — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 25. Lecture original.




A mid-sentence cut leaves “11:59pm” on a card that no longer says what is due. Overlap saves the join. A heading-aware split keeps “Grading — Milestone” with the date.


Contextual retrieval
Even a clean chunk can be meaningless on its own. “The company’s revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter” does not say which company or which quarter. Anthropic’s contextual retrieval prepends a short situating line, written by a model from the whole document, before the chunk is embedded and indexed. The query “What was the revenue growth for ACME Corp in Q2 2023?” can then match the card.







Figure 2: A bare chunk versus the same chunk with a situating preface — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 26. The ACME figures are a lecture illustration of the idea in Anthropic’s contextual retrieval.




The method is a prompt over the whole document and the chunk: ask for a short context that situates the chunk for search, and store that prefix with the text. Anthropic also combines the contextual embedding with a contextual BM25 index, so meaning and exact terms can vote together — a hybrid we will meet again on the retrievers page.
On their evaluation, as shown in the lecture, average failed retrievals at 20 fall from 5.7% (embedding only) and 5.0% (embedding plus BM25) to 3.7% with contextual embeddings and 2.9% with contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25. Those are Anthropic’s reported failure rates, not a rerun of our own. The relative drop from 5.7% to 2.9% is the “about 49%” reduction that the blog highlights.







Figure 3: Average failed retrievals at 20, with and without contextual embeddings and contextual BM25 — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 29. Original: Anthropic, Contextual Retrieval.




Late chunking (Günther et al., 2024) is a different way to give a chunk document context. You embed the whole document with a long-context encoder, then mean-pool the token vectors that fall inside each chunk’s span. There is no extra language-model call and no added prefix on the stored text: the context lives in the vector.


When one chunk is not enough
Some questions are about a theme, not a sentence. RAPTOR — Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval (Sarthi et al.) — builds a tree from the bottom up: embed the chunks, cluster them, summarise each cluster with a language model, embed the summaries, and repeat. A detail question can match a leaf; a thematic question can match a node. The lecture labels this Sarthi et al., 2025; the paper appeared in 2024 (arXiv, January 2024; ICLR 2024).







Figure 4: RAPTOR builds a tree of summaries above the chunks, and retrieves across levels — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 32. Original: RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024). The lecture writes 2025; the paper is from 2024.




GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) is a cousin for questions that need a global view of a corpus. At index time an LLM extracts entities and relations, builds a knowledge graph, and detects communities. At query time it writes community summaries and then a global answer. Later surveys of graph-based RAG, such as Han et al. (2025), collect the many variants of that idea.







Figure 5: GraphRAG: a knowledge graph and its communities at index time, query-focused summaries at read time — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 34. Original: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization (Edge et al., 2024).






Finding a vector quickly
Once every chunk is a vector, the query is a nearest-neighbour search: given a query vector, return the top-\(k\) of \(N\) chunk vectors. An exact scan costs \(O(N \cdot d)\) per query. Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) methods trade a little recall for a lot of speed. The lecture’s short list is inverted-file indexes (cluster, then probe nearby centroids), product quantisation (compress each vector into a short code), and HNSW — hierarchical navigable small worlds (Malkov and Yashunin).
HNSW is a multi-layer proximity graph: every vector lives on the bottom layer, thinner samples live above. Search starts at the top, hops greedily toward the query, and drops a layer when it is stuck. In the usual picture you pay about \(\log N\) hops and keep high recall. The index is built by inserting one vector at a time, placing most nodes only on the bottom layer, and linking each to a few neighbours plus a longer-range edge so a greedy walk cannot get trapped.







Figure 6: HNSW: a stack of proximity graphs, coarse at the top and complete at the bottom — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 37. The idea follows Malkov and Yashunin. Lecture original.






In one table







Choice
What it is for




Fixed-size chunks, with overlap
A simple default; overlap reduces mid-sentence cuts


Structure-aware cuts
Keep headings and sections together


Contextual retrieval
A short preface, so a chunk names its document and moment


Late chunking
Pool a long-context embedding over each chunk’s span


RAPTOR
A tree of summaries, for questions that span many chunks


GraphRAG
A graph of entities and communities, for corpus-level questions


HNSW (and other ANN)
Fast approximate search over a large vector index





FAQ
Is there one right chunk size? No. The lecture’s 100–500 token band is a starting range, not a law. Too short starves the vector; too long mixes topics. You measure, as you would any other index choice.
Do I need an LLM call for every chunk? Only if you use a method like contextual retrieval. Late chunking gets document context from the encoder itself. A heading and a filename, stored as metadata, are sometimes enough.
Why not embed the whole document as one vector? Because a single vector is a blur, and because most questions match a passage, not a book. Trees and graphs are there for the questions that do need a wider view.
Where does this meet retrieval? Indexing decides what a “passage” is. Retrievers decide how a query finds it: sparse overlap, a dense vector, or something in between.

title: LLMs for agents
text:
The typist in a loop






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


The last part of Lecture 2 is the bridge back to Lecture 1. You now have a next-token model, an architecture, a training recipe, and an inference engine. An agent is that model in a loop, talking to tools, files, and other components. Two practical problems show up immediately: the parts need a contract for how they talk, and the model’s context window is a scarce, slightly unreliable working memory.






Everyday example



Picture a busy office again. The clerk from Lecture 1 can write letters, but the office only works if the forms have a fixed layout (structured input and output), if you do not dump the entire filing cabinet on the desk (context rot), and if you add new papers to the end of the pile so nobody has to reshuffle what was already in hand (the KV cache). A short list of tools — a folder, a pen, a terminal — often beats a wall of rarely used gadgets.




Structured input and output
Zaharia and colleagues, in the BAIR note we already used on Compound AI systems, put it plainly: more and more results come from compound systems, not from a single model call. Those systems need a shared contract for how the parts communicate.







Figure 1: From a single model to a compound system that needs a contract between its parts — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 152. Original: Compound AI Systems (Zaharia et al., BAIR, 18 February 2024).




One way to enforce the contract is constrained decoding: you only let the model emit tokens that fit a grammar or a finite-state machine, so the output is valid JSON, a legal tool call, or a DSPy-shaped record. SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) is the lecture’s example: it uses finite-state machines, among other systems tricks, to keep structured generation fast. DSPy signatures are a higher-level version of the same idea: you declare the fields you want, and the framework takes care of getting the model to fill them.
You can also constrain the model outside free text generation. A small classifier head on embeddings can map a state to a label. The lecture mentions a current slogan, “System One” models: roughly, classifiers with adaptable options, used for decisions rather than for open-ended prose (the lecture points at contrastive-lm.notion.site). And for tools, the ancestor paper is Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023): a language model that learns, from its own traces, when to call an API and how to put the result back into the text.


Context engineering
Prompt engineering was about the wording of a single request. Context engineering is about everything that goes into the window of an agent over a long run. The lecture’s picture is from Anthropic’s Effective context engineering for AI agents.







Figure 2: Prompt engineering for a single turn, versus curating what of a much larger possible context actually enters an agent’s window — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 161. Original: Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents.




What might go in that window? The lecture’s list is short and complete enough to start from:

the system prompt
the message history
memories
tool-call results
attached files

The temptation is to put all of it in, every time. That is usually a mistake.


Context rot, bloat, and the cache
Longer is not always better. Oolong (the lecture stylises the name as OOLONG) measures long-context reasoning and aggregation: as the context grows, scores fall, on both synthetic and more realistic splits. The lecture uses that plot as a warning labelled context rot.







Figure 3: Context rot: scores on Oolong drop as the context gets longer, rather than staying flat out to the advertised window — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 164. Original: Oolong: Evaluating Long Context Reasoning and Aggregation Capabilities. The lecture writes the name as OOLONG; the paper’s title is Oolong.




The lecture’s practical advice, which students also meet in the course homework, is that there is no single right context. You experiment. A few concrete habits help:

Avoid bloat. Sometimes a few tools are enough. The lecture points at Pi, which exposes just read, write, edit, and bash — a case made in The harness tax on arena.ai. Recovery of the rest can wait for retrieval, which is the subject of Why RAG and Indexing for RAG.
Add sequentially. If you insert or edit tokens earlier in the context, the positional embeddings of everything after them change, and the KV cache for that suffix is invalidated. Append new material where you can, so prefill work is not thrown away. This is the inference engine leaking into the agent’s bookkeeping.
Evaluate the choices empirically. Toolformer is the lecture’s reminder that you can set up tests and measure whether a context change helped, rather than arguing from taste.
Compact carefully. By the time you compact, the context is already very long. Keep too much and you will have to compact again soon; drop too much and you lose what the task still needs.








Figure 4: Inserting or editing earlier tokens changes later positional embeddings and invalidates the KV cache for the suffix — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 169. Lecture original.






A different philosophy: recursive language models
Instead of stuffing a huge window, recursive language models treat the context as something the model can explore with its own sub-calls: look at a slice, recurse, and only bring back what is needed. The paper is Recursive Language Models (2025); the lecture also credits Alex Zhang’s write-up. On one Oolong setting in that write-up, an RLM built on a smaller model can outscore a larger model used in the ordinary way, and outscore a ReAct baseline. Those bar heights are the source’s numbers, not a rerun of our own.







Figure 5: Recursive LMs on one Oolong setting with a 263k-token context, as reported by the source — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 173. Original: Recursive Language Models (see also arXiv:2512.24601).






In one table







Habit
Why it matters




Structured I/O
Compound systems need a contract, not free-form prose between every part


Constrained decoding
Enforce the contract at sample time (FSMs, grammars, DSPy signatures)


Small decision models
Classifiers, or “System One” heads, for some choices instead of a long generation


Context engineering
Curate the window: system prompt, history, memories, tool results, files


Context rot
Longer contexts can hurt; measure, do not assume


Few tools, then retrieval
Avoid harness bloat; recover extras when needed


Append, do not reshuffle
Protect the KV cache


Compaction / recursion
When the window is full, summarise carefully — or let the model recurse into the text





FAQ
Is context engineering just a new name for prompt engineering? It is a wider job. Prompt engineering is usually a single wording. Context engineering is the running policy for what an agent can see: what you include, what you retrieve, what you drop, and when you compact.
Why not always use the model’s maximum context? Because the model may not use that length well. Oolong is the lecture’s exhibit: quality can fall as you fill the window, even inside the advertised limit.
Why does editing the system prompt mid-run get expensive? The prompt is a prefix. Change it, and every later position shifts, so the cache built for that suffix is no longer valid. You pay a fresh prefill. This is one reason to keep stable instructions stable, and to append results at the end.
What is coming next in the course? The lecture ends with “see you on Wednesday for RAG.” Retrieval is the systematic way to keep the window small and still reach a large store of files and memories. That lecture is now a set of pages starting at Why RAG.

title: History of agents
text:
The word is older than the models






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


The word agent comes from the Latin agens: one who acts. That is a late-fifteenth-century sense, and it is still the right starting point. A thermostat acts. A trading program acts. A language model that only completes a prompt does not, on its own, act in the world: it writes tokens. The interesting story is how “agent” moved from a word for a person who acts on someone else’s behalf, into AI, into reinforcement learning, and then, quite suddenly, onto a language model that can plan, call a tool, and look at the result.
This page is the history. The next three pages take the architecture, the compound systems around an LLM, and the open problems.






Everyday example



Think of a junior clerk in an office. At first they only copy letters (a language model with no tools). Then someone gives them a telephone, a filing cabinet, and a list of people they may call. Now they can do things: look something up, ring a supplier, write down what happened, and decide the next step. The clerk is the same person. What changed is the loop around them: observe, think, act, remember. That is the move this history is about.




A causal timeline





flowchart TD
  H["1973: Hewitt, Bishop and Steiger, ACTOR formalism"] --> N["1980: Contract Net Protocol"]
  N --> M["1986: Minsky, Society of Mind"]
  M --> D["1990s: Maes; Wooldridge and Jennings; Russell and Norvig"]
  D --> R["1998: Sutton and Barto, the agent–environment loop"]
  R --> Q["2015: DQN on Atari"]
  Q --> G["2020: GPT-3 and in-context learning"]
  G --> K["2022: MRKL and ReAct"]
  K --> C["2022–23: ChatGPT, then public agent loops"]






Each step is a reason for the next, not just a date on a poster. Actors needed a way to talk about independent processes that send messages. Negotiation protocols needed a way for those processes to hand off work. Cognitive metaphors and textbook definitions made “agent” a standard unit of AI. Reinforcement learning gave the unit a loop and a reward. Deep RL showed that the loop could learn hard games from pixels. Large language models then made the “think” step cheap to write in English, and tool use made the “act” step reach outside the model.


Before 1990
CS 329Z Lecture 1 points to A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence (Hewitt, Bishop and Steiger, IJCAI 1973) as an early indexed use of agent in AI. The paper is about actors: independent computational entities that communicate by passing messages. That is already a step away from “one big program that knows everything”.







Figure 1: The first page of Hewitt, Bishop and Steiger’s ACTOR formalism paper (IJCAI 1973) — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 19. Original: A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence.




In 1980 the Contract Net Protocol (Smith) described how such agents could negotiate tasks: announce work, bid, award a contract. The picture is a small labour market, not a single controller with a fixed plan.
In 1986 Marvin Minsky published The Society of Mind. Intelligence, in that book, is not one homunculus. It is a society of simpler processes whose interactions add up to something that looks like a mind. You can see the rhyme with later multi-agent designs, even if the mechanisms are different.







Figure 2: Smith’s Contract Net Protocol (1980) and Minsky’s The Society of Mind (1986) — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 20. Originals: The Contract Net Protocol (Smith, 1980); Minsky, The Society of Mind, 1986.






The 1990s: trying to say what an agent is
By the mid-1990s the word needed a definition, because everyone was using it.

Pattie Maes, in work collected as Designing Autonomous Agents (1994), is a standard pointer for agents that act in a world with some independence from a human operator.
Wooldridge and Jennings (1995) gave a widely cited cluster of properties: autonomy, social ability, reactivity, and proactiveness. An agent is not only a function from an input to an output. It has its own thread of control, it can deal with other agents, it responds to what just happened, and it can take the initiative.
The first edition of Russell and Norvig’s Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (1995) made a cleaner, more operational definition: an agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through actuators. A thermostat counts. So does a robot. So, later, does a language model with tools.

Those three views are not in conflict so much as they are at different zoom levels. Russell and Norvig give you a test you can apply to a thermostat. Wooldridge and Jennings tell you what people usually mean when they want something richer than a thermostat.







Figure 3: Three 1990s definitions of an agent: Maes (1994), Wooldridge and Jennings (1995), and Russell and Norvig — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 21. The lecture cites the 1995 first-edition definition; the cover shown is a later edition. Originals: Maes, Designing Autonomous Agents, 1994; Wooldridge and Jennings (1995); Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach.






The reinforcement-learning era
Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (Sutton and Barto, 1998) put the agent–environment loop at the centre of a textbook: at each step the agent observes a state, chooses an action, and receives a next state and a reward. The goal is to learn a policy that accumulates reward. For a couple of decades, when someone in machine learning said “agent”, this was often what they meant.
The loop became famous again when deep networks started to learn it from raw observations. Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning (Mnih et al., 2015) trained a deep Q-network on Atari games from pixels and scores. The agent was no longer a hand-built controller with a small state table. It was a network that improved by playing.
That success is part of why today’s language-model agents still talk about observations, actions, and environments. The objects changed — a web page instead of a game screen, a tool call instead of a joystick — but the loop did not.







Figure 4: The agent–environment loop and a deep Q-network on Atari — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 22. Originals: the loop from Sutton and Barto (1998); the network diagram from Mnih et al., 2015. The slide also shows AlphaGo and an OpenAI / OG event graphic.






The language-model era
Two things had to happen before “LLM agent” became a common phrase.
First, the models had to be able to change their behaviour from the prompt alone. Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (Brown et al., 2020) showed that GPT-3 could pick up a new format or a new task from a handful of examples in context, without a gradient step. Once you can teach a model a pattern in the prompt, you can also teach it a procedure: think, then act, then look at the result.







Figure 5: A Transformer and GPT-3-style in-context learning — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 23. Originals: the architecture is Figure 1 of Vaswani et al., 2017; the few-shot prompt is from Brown et al., 2020.




Second, people started to wrap the model in other components. MRKL Systems (Karpas et al., 2022) argued for a modular, neuro-symbolic design: a language model plus external knowledge sources and discrete reasoners, rather than asking the model to do everything in its parameters. That is already a compound system, even if the word “agent” is not yet on every slide.
Then the loop was written out in the model’s own language. ReAct (Yao, Zhao, Yu, Du, Shafran, Narasimhan and Cao; arXiv, October 2022) interleaved reasoning traces with actions and observations. The model does not only answer. It can decide to search, read what came back, think again, and only then commit. The lecture treats this paper as the hinge between “an LLM that reasons” and “an LLM that acts”.
Public systems arrived in a hurry around the same time. ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022. GPT-4 was announced on 14 March 2023. In late March 2023, public loops such as BabyAGI and AutoGPT made the same idea tangible for a much wider audience: give a model a goal, let it propose the next step, let it use tools, repeat. Capability was moving; so was attention.







Figure 6: A 2022–23 timeline from ReAct to public agent loops — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 25. The ReAct trace is from Yao et al., 2022; the BabyAGI diagram is from yoheinakajima/babyagi_archive.




What followed is less a single invention than a tightening of the same loop: better models, better tools, longer memory, more evaluation. The architecture of that loop is the next page. The compound systems around it are on Compound AI systems. The problems that appeared as soon as the loops left the demo — reliability, training, evaluation, safety — are on Key challenges.

FAQ
Is a language model already an agent? Not by itself, if you take the word in the Russell and Norvig sense. A frozen model maps a prompt to tokens. It becomes agent-like when you put it in a loop with observations and actions — tools, a browser, a codebase, a user.
Did “agent” in AI start with ChatGPT? No. The lecture is careful about this. The word has a long AI history: actors, negotiation protocols, textbook definitions, reinforcement learning. What changed in 2022–23 was that the policy could be a large language model, and the actions could be tool calls written in text.
Why does ReAct sit at the centre of the recent story? Because it made the loop explicit in the model’s own generations: a thought, an action, an observation, another thought. Later designs add memory, more tools, or several agents, but they are still variations on that skeleton. See Agent architectures.
Where should I read next, besides the lecture? Lilian Weng’s LLM Powered Autonomous Agents (23 June 2023) is a clear survey of planning, memory, and tools. For the move from a single model to a system, see Zaharia et al., The Shift from Models to Compound AI Systems (BAIR, 18 February 2024). For how we know whether an agent is actually useful, see Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir and Narayanan, AI Agents That Matter (arXiv, July 2024).

title: Key challenges in building agents
text:
When the demo is not the system






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


An agent that looks good in a one-shot demo can still fail as soon as it has to run for more than a few steps, on a slightly different task, in front of a person who did not write the prompt. CS 329Z Lecture 1 groups the open problems under five headings: reliability, training, long-horizon behaviour, safety, and evaluation. They overlap, but they are not the same complaint.





flowchart TD
  Rel["Reliability: errors compound"]
  Train["Training: sparse reward, long horizon, costly rollouts"]
  Hor["Long horizon: context grows and drifts"]
  Saf["Safety: finishing the task is not the same as behaving well"]
  Ev["Evaluation: what to measure, and how"]












Everyday example



A single typo in a one-line email is an annoyance. The same typo in a ten-step travel booking — wrong date copied into the hotel, then into the invoice, then into the calendar — becomes a ruined trip. Agents live in that second world. Each step takes the last step as input, so a small mistake does not stay small. That is why reliability, evaluation, and safety have to be designed for trajectories, not only for single answers.




Reliability, and why evaluation has to measure it
Errors compound in an agent setup. A slightly wrong tool call produces a slightly wrong observation, which produces a worse thought, which produces a worse act. A system that is “usually fine” at each step can still be unreliable over a full task.
The lecture asks three evaluation questions that are easy to skip if you only report a success rate:

Consistency across runs. If you give the agent the same task twice, does it reach the same outcome?
Robustness to perturbations. If you make a small, realistic change to the prompt, the tools, or the environment, does the behaviour hold?
Predictable failure. When it fails, is the failure legible and recoverable, or does it fail in a way you cannot anticipate?








Figure 1: Three reliability questions for agent evaluation — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 62. The slide points to the Holistic Agent Leaderboard.




These are reliability questions, and they are also evaluation questions. A leaderboard that only counts “task completed” will not show you any of them. The lecture points to the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and its reliability dashboard as a public attempt to make that gap visible — a capability–reliability gap: agents can look able, and still not be dependable.







Figure 2: A snapshot of the HAL reliability dashboard, as shown in the lecture — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 63. Original: HAL Reliability Dashboard. Figures on the live dashboard may change.




Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir and Narayanan, AI Agents That Matter (arXiv, 1 July 2024), make a complementary argument about current agent benchmarks: too much weight on accuracy, not enough on cost; model-developer and application-developer needs mixed together; weak or missing holdouts, so agents overfit the benchmark; and evaluation practice that is hard to reproduce. Their title is the point. We want agents that matter in use, not only agents that climb a board.


Training, and the long horizon
Training an agent is hard for reasons that reinforcement learning already knew about, and that language-model loops have not removed.

Sparse reward. Feedback often arrives at the end of a long attempt, if it arrives at all. Most tokens and tool calls get no direct signal.
Long horizon. The task takes many steps. Credit assignment — which thought actually helped? — becomes a guess.
Expensive rollouts. Each attempt may mean many model calls, many tool calls, and a live environment. You cannot cheaply sample a million games in a simulator if the “game” is a cloud account or a colleague’s inbox.

Long-horizon behaviour is also a systems problem at inference time, not only a training one. The context grows. Early goals drift or get crowded out. The agent may forget the constraint you stated at the top, or spend its window on a raw log instead of a useful memory. That is why the architecture page spends time on episodic, semantic, and procedural memory: without some way to write down and retrieve what matters, a long run is just a short run with more tokens in the way.


Safety: finishing the task is not enough
The lecture’s slogan is easy to remember and easy to ignore in a demo: task success is not the same as safe behaviour. An agent can book the hotel, edit the repo, or send the email, and still have done something you would not have allowed.







Figure 3: Task completion is not the same as safety compliance — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 64. Original: HarnessAudit Bench.




A few concrete lines of evidence the lecture points to:

HarnessAudit is a benchmark aimed at this gap: whether a harness complies with safety requirements, not only whether a task completes.
Agents that share a computer with a person can lack a sense of when not to act, or of what the person is in the middle of. The lecture points to a hands-on write-up of an early computer-use agent (Platformer on OpenAI’s Operator) as a picture of missing collaboration awareness.
Visual attacks can be almost boring, and still work. Attacking Vision-Language Computer Agents via Pop-ups (Zhang, Yu and Yang, 2024) shows that carefully designed pop-ups — the kind a person would usually recognise and ignore — can draw a vision-language agent into clicking them instead of finishing the task. In OSWorld and VisualWebArena the authors report an average attack success rate (the agent clicking the pop-ups) of 86%, and a 47% drop in task success. Simple defences such as “ignore pop-ups”, or an advertisement notice, did not fix it. (The lecture slide rounds the first of those figures; the numbers above are from the paper.)








Figure 4: Adversarial pop-ups that can pull a vision-language agent off its task, on OSWorld and VisualWebArena — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 66. Original: Zhang, Yu and Yang, 2024. The environment click rates are from that paper; the lecture’s combined headline was rounded, and is omitted from the crop.





Privacy is a behaviour, not only a policy document. PrivacyLens (Shao, Li, Shi, Liu and Yang, NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks 2024) evaluates whether language models respect privacy norms in action, not only when asked a static question.








Figure 5: A privacy failure in action: an agent drafts an email that leaks a private lunch — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 67. Original: PrivacyLens (Shao, Li, Shi, Liu and Yang, NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks 2024).





Misalignment and sycophancy — telling you what you seem to want, or exploiting a reward signal — remain live issues once an agent can act. The lecture points to Anthropic’s write-up of reward tampering research.
Multi-agent collusion is a newer shape of the same worry: several agents, or an agent and another system, can interact in ways no single-agent test would show. The lecture points to a METR investigation (26 August 2026) as a recent case to learn from, rather than as a folklore story.








Figure 6: A picture of multi-agent collusion on a shared message board — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 69. Original: METR’s investigation (26 August 2026), with Redwood Research.




None of these replaces a safety case for your own system. They are a reminder that “it completed the issue” is an incomplete report.

Challenge
The short version
A place to look

HAL reliability dashboard


Training

The RL-era loop on the history page

Memory types in Agent architectures

Task completion is not safe behaviour
HarnessAudit, PrivacyLens, Zhang et al., 2024


Evaluation
What you measure, and how you hold it out
Kapoor et al., 2024





FAQ
Can I fix reliability just by using a stronger model? A stronger core can help, and it can also fail faster, or more confidently, in the same loop. Reliability here is a property of the system: tools, validation, memory, retries, and how you measure them. That is why the compound systems page insists on the three layers — system, data, and evals — rather than only on the model.
Why is evaluation listed separately from reliability? Because you can evaluate the wrong thing very carefully. A benchmark that rewards a costly, fragile agent for a slightly higher success rate will push the field in the wrong direction. Kapoor et al. argue for looking at cost together with accuracy, for keeping model evaluation and application evaluation distinct, and for holdouts that make overfitting visible.
Is “the agent got the task right” a safety result? No. That is the lecture’s point, and it is why HarnessAudit, PrivacyLens, and the pop-up attacks are on this page together. You need checks for the behaviour you didn’t want, including on runs that look like successes.
What should I read alongside the lecture? Kapoor et al., AI Agents That Matter; Weng, LLM Powered Autonomous Agents, for the architecture these problems sit on; and Zaharia et al., The Shift from Models to Compound AI Systems, for why the unit of work is the system.

title: Lab#FU01-2: Taxi fare, NumPy and scikit-learn
text:
📘 Lab#FU01-2: Taxi fare, NumPy and scikit-learn
In this lab you will:

Load more receipts, with a pickup fee as well as a rate per kilometre.
Run gradient descent in NumPy for both \(w\) and \(b\).
Plot the loss, and how \(w\) and \(b\) settle.
Compare your result with LinearRegression from scikit-learn.

   Code on GitHub

Lab#FU01-1 learned one number: the fare per kilometre. A real taxi also has a flag fall — the bit you pay before the metres start to run. The model is now
\[
\text{price} = w \cdot \text{km} + b
\]
True values on these receipts: \(w = 1.50\), \(b = 2.00\). The program is not told those two numbers. The loop does not change: predict, measure the error, nudge each parameter, repeat.
The editor below is live Python in the browser. The first load takes a few seconds, because it also fetches NumPy and scikit-learn.

1 Creating the algorithm
The question. A taxi charges a rate per kilometre and a fixed pickup fee. We have eight receipts, from 1 km at €3.50 to 12 km at €20. What does 7 km cost? We don’t know the rate or the fee, so we let the receipts teach both to us.
# TODO: find the price of a 7 km trip from eight receipts
Why one number isn’t enough. In Lab#FU01-1 the fare was just price = w · km. That cannot fit these receipts: 1 km at €3.50 would mean a rate of €3.50 / km, but 12 km at €20 would mean about €1.67 / km. We need a second number, the flag fall. The model is now price = w · km + b. Two unknowns: the rate w and the base fare b.
# TODO: price = w * km + b; both w and b are unknown
What we know and what we don’t. We know the kilometres (the input) and the prices (the answers). We store them as NumPy arrays, so we can add and multiply the whole list in one go, with no for loop. We don’t know w or b.
import numpy as np

km    = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 12.0])  # inputs
price = np.array([3.50, 5.00, 6.50, 9.50, 11.00, 14.00, 17.00, 20.00])  # answers
# TODO: w and b are unknown, the things to learn
A first guess. We have no idea, so we start badly on purpose and watch both numbers improve.
w = 0.0                  # a bad guess on purpose
b = 0.0
Predict. With our guess, what would each trip cost? With w = 0 and b = 0, every trip comes out free. NumPy multiplies the whole array at once.
pred = w * km + b        # [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
How wrong are we? We compare each prediction with the real receipt, square the gaps, and average them. That number is the loss, and we want it small. NumPy does it in one line.
loss = np.mean((pred - price)**2)
Which way to move? Every prediction was too low, so both w and b must go up. We now have two gradients. The one for w still multiplies by kilometres, because a change in the rate matters more on a long trip. The one for b does not: the flag fall is the same on every ride, short or long.
grad_w = np.mean(2 * (pred - price) * km)
grad_b = np.mean(2 * (pred - price))
A small step. We nudge both numbers a little that way. The learning rate is the step size: too small and we crawl, too big and we bounce past the bottom.
lr = 0.01
w = w - lr * grad_w
b = b - lr * grad_b
Again and again. We predict, measure and nudge, over and over. It takes many more steps than Lab 1: w and b pull on each other, so a step that helps the rate can undo some of the fee, and the other way around. After 500 steps we are close; after 2000 steps we are there.
for step in range(2000):
    # predict, measure, find both directions, step
    ...
When to stop. We stop when the loss barely changes, or after a fixed number of steps.
# TODO: stop when loss < 0.0001, or after N steps
Check the answer. w ≈ 1.50 and b ≈ 2.00, so 7 km costs about €12.50. We also ask scikit-learn’s LinearRegression for the same fit: a trusted reference, in closed form, with no loop. It lands on the same two numbers. Nobody told the program the rate or the fee; it found them from examples. That’s learning.
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit(km.reshape(-1, 1), price)
# model.coef_ ≈ 1.50,  model.intercept_ ≈ 2.00
print(w * 7 + b)         # ≈ 12.50


2 More receipts, then two parameters
Eight rides, all generated from \(1.5 \cdot \text{km} + 2\). The derivative of the mean squared error with respect to \(w\) is the average of \(2 \cdot \text{error} \cdot \text{km}\). With respect to \(b\), it is the average of \(2 \cdot \text{error}\). Start at \(w = 0\), \(b = 0\), and take \(2000\) steps of size \(0.01\). Two parameters take more steps than one.






Try it



Change learning_rate and press Run. Try a smaller rate, or a larger one. You can also try fewer steps and watch \(w\) and \(b\) stop short of 1.50 and 2.00.








After 500 steps the fit is already close (\(w \approx 1.514\), \(b \approx 1.887\)). After 2000 steps, \(w = 1.500004\) and \(b = 1.999971\). LinearRegression lands on the true \(w\) and \(b\). The two lines sit on top of each other. That is the point: your loop and the library are doing the same job. The library is faster and more stable; the loop is the one you can see.


3 What you should notice
Two parameters are coupled, so the walk toward the true \(w\) and \(b\) is slower than Lab 1. A learning rate of \(0.01\) is still safe here, but you need many more steps. In later labs you will scale the inputs and use better updates.


4 See also

title: The learning loop
text:
A real example with one weight: taxi fare
Price = w · kilometres, and w is unknown. You have three receipts: 2 km for €3, 5 km for €7.50, 10 km for €15. The true rate is €1.50 per kilometre, but nobody tells the model that.
The loop is the same one you will see in the code below.

Guess: start with \(w = 0\) — every ride is free.
Predict: €0, €0, €0.
Measure: off by €3, €7.50, and €15.
Nudge: the derivative says go up. With a learning rate of \(0.01\), \(w\) jumps to \(1.29\).
Repeat: \(1.47\), then \(1.496\), then about \(1.50\).

In three or four steps it has learned €1.50/km from three receipts. Nobody programmed the rate.








The taxi loop: guess, predict, measure the error, nudge w, and repeat, until w reaches €1.50 / km.











The taxi loop: guess, predict, measure the error, nudge w, and repeat, until w reaches €1.50 / km.



A bias (\(y = w\cdot x + b\)) would learn a pickup fee as well, the bit you pay before the metres start to run.
You can run this loop yourself in Lab#FU01-1: Taxi fare, pure Python. Lab#FU01-2 adds the pickup fee and compares your descent with scikit-learn.

The fare per kilometre climbs from 0 to €1.50 in a few steps.





A real-world example: a spam filter
A spam filter is the same loop, with thousands of weights instead of one.
It starts by guessing that every word matters equally. It predicts spam or not for each email, then measures the error against emails that people have already marked as spam. It nudges the weights: “free money” goes up, “meeting tomorrow” goes down. Then it repeats, millions of times.
Google Maps arrival times and Netflix recommendations work the same way: guess, check against reality, adjust, repeat.


The simplest model
The simplest model is a single weight: \(y = w \cdot x\). We give it data where the true answer is \(w = 2\) (\(y\) is always \(2\times x\)) and watch it find that on its own.


The learning loop

Guess: start with \(w = 0\).
Predict: compute \(w \cdot x\) for each example.
Measure the error: how far off are the predictions? (squared error)
Nudge \(w\) in the direction that reduces the error (the derivative says which way).
Repeat.







Everyday example



You season a soup. Taste it: too little salt. Add a pinch, taste again. You do not dump the whole shaker — that would ruin it. That pinch is the learning rate; tasting and nudging, over and over, is how a model learns.







flowchart TD
  A[Start with a guess] --> B[Predict]
  B --> C[Measure the squared error]
  C --> D[Nudge the weight]
  D --> B








The code
The data is \(x=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(y=\{2,4,6,8\}\). The learning rate is \(0.01\), for \(20\) steps.

JavaPython


public class Learn {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double[] x = {1, 2, 3, 4};
        double[] y = {2, 4, 6, 8};   // y = 2 * x
        double w = 0;                // initial guess
        double lr = 0.01;            // learning rate (step size)

        for (int step = 0; step < 20; step++) {
            double grad = 0, loss = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < x.length; i++) {
                double err = w * x[i] - y[i];
                loss += err * err;
                grad += 2 * err * x[i];   // derivative of err² with respect to w
            }
            loss /= x.length;
            grad /= x.length;

            w -= lr * grad;              // the learning step
            System.out.printf("step %d  w=%.3f  loss=%.4f%n", step, w, loss);
        }
    }
}


x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
y = [2, 4, 6, 8]   # y = 2 * x
w = 0.0            # initial guess
lr = 0.01          # learning rate (step size)

for step in range(20):
    grad = 0.0
    loss = 0.0
    for i in range(len(x)):
        err = w * x[i] - y[i]
        loss += err * err
        grad += 2 * err * x[i]   # derivative of err**2 with respect to w
    loss /= len(x)
    grad /= len(x)
    w -= lr * grad               # the learning step
    print(f"step {step}  w={w:.3f}  loss={loss:.4f}")





What you’ll see
\(w\) starts at \(0\), jumps to \(0.3\) after the first step, then climbs toward \(2\) while the loss shrinks toward \(0\). That is learning: no one told it “\(2\)”, it found it by repeatedly reducing its own error.
A real run of the program above prints this (the loss on each line is the error before that step’s nudge):
step 0  w=0.300  loss=30.0000
step 1  w=0.555  loss=21.6750
step 2  w=0.772  loss=15.6602
step 3  w=0.956  loss=11.3145
step 4  w=1.113  loss=8.1747
...
step 18  w=1.909  loss=0.0863
step 19  w=1.922  loss=0.0624
After twenty steps, \(w\) is \(1.922\), already close to \(2\).








The weight climbs toward 2, and the squared error falls toward 0.











The weight climbs toward 2, and the squared error falls toward 0.





Try this
Change lr and run it again. The step size really matters.

lr = 0.001 — slow learning. After twenty steps, \(w\) is only \(0.522\) and the printed loss is still \(16.8927\).
lr = 0.1 — the first nudge overshoots: \(w\) jumps to \(3.000\), then zig-zags (\(1.500\), \(2.250\), \(1.875\), ) but it still converges, and faster than \(0.01\).
lr = 0.2 — it blows up. \(w\) goes \(6\), \(-6\), \(18\), \(-30\), and the loss keeps growing.

# lr = 0.1
step 0  w=3.000  loss=30.0000
step 1  w=1.500  loss=7.5000
step 2  w=2.250  loss=1.8750
step 3  w=1.875  loss=0.4688

# lr = 0.2
step 0  w=6.000  loss=30.0000
step 1  w=-6.000  loss=120.0000
step 2  w=18.000  loss=480.0000
The nudge itself is the same idea as on the optimization page: \(w \leftarrow w - \eta\nabla L\). The gradient says which way.


Why this is so relevant, and why we say a machine is learning
This little loop is so relevant because it is the same loop behind every neural network: an MNIST classifier, a large language model, all of them. Only the scale changes — more weights, more data, a longer chain. The idea does not.
Why do we say the machine is learning? Nobody programmed \(w = 2\). We did not write the rule y = 2 * x. The program started from a wrong guess and improved its own performance from data and experience, by reducing its error, step after step.
Tom Mitchell put it this way in 1997:

A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.

Here the task \(T\) is to predict \(y\) from \(x\), the performance \(P\) is the squared error (smaller is better), and the experience \(E\) is the four examples. After twenty steps, \(P\) has improved. So we call it learning.






Everyday example



You learn to throw a dart, or to ride a bike, in the same way: you miss, you correct, you try again. Nobody hands you a finished list of rules. The machine is doing that, with a number \(w\).


An ordinary program works like this: you write the rules, you give it data, and it produces answers. Machine learning flips the arrow: you give it data and the answers, and it finds the rules.








An ordinary program is rules plus data, giving answers. Machine learning is data plus answers, giving rules.











An ordinary program is rules plus data, giving answers. Machine learning is data plus answers, giving rules.





Next step: a bias
Next step would be adding a bias: \(y = w\cdot x + b\). Now two numbers have to be learned, not one, but the loop does not change: predict, measure the error, nudge each parameter, repeat. That is Lab#FU01-2: Taxi fare, NumPy and scikit-learn.

title: Probability and statistics essentials
text:
Random variables and distributions
A random variable is a number whose value depends on a random outcome: the face of a die, a pixel, a class label.
A distribution says how likely each value is. The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the familiar bell curve, written \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\): \(\mu\) is the centre, \(\sigma\) is the spread. Many residuals and many “noise” models are assumed to be roughly normal. GELU, on the activation-functions page, even uses the standard normal CDF \(\Phi\).


Expectation, variance, and standard deviation
The expectation \(\mathbb{E}[x]\) is the probability-weighted average. For a fair die it is \(3.5\). For a dataset, the same idea becomes an ordinary mean: add the values, divide by \(n\).
Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean: “how spread out?”. The standard deviation \(\sigma\) is the square root of the variance, so it lives in the same units as \(x\). Careful: in a network diagram the letter \(\sigma\) often means the sigmoid instead; see the symbols page.
A tiny example. For the two values \([2,4]\), the mean is \(3\). Each value sits \(1\) away from \(3\), so the (population) variance is \(1\) and \(\sigma=1\).
import numpy as np
x = np.array([2.0, 4.0])
x.mean(), x.var(), x.std()   # 3.0, 1.0, 1.0


Mean and median
The mean is the ordinary average. The median is the middle value once the numbers are sorted. The mean is pulled by outliers; the median is calmer.
A tiny example. For \([10,12,13,15,100]\), the mean is \(30\) and the median is \(13\). One large value dragged the mean a long way; the middle of the list did not move.


Conditional probability and Bayes
Conditional probability \(P(A\mid B)\) is “the probability of \(A\), given that we already know \(B\)”. Bayes’ rule turns the evidence around:
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}.
\]
A tiny example. \(100\) emails, \(20\) of them spam. The word “prize” appears in \(16\) of the spam emails and in \(8\) of the rest, so in \(24\) emails altogether.
\[
P(\text{spam}\mid\text{prize})=\frac{(16/20)\cdot(20/100)}{24/100}=\frac{16}{24}=\frac{2}{3}.
\]
Seeing “prize” does not prove spam, but it raises the chance from \(20\%\) to about \(67\%\). This is the same arithmetic that Naïve Bayes uses, with a simplifying assumption that features are independent given the class.


Likelihood, and why cross-entropy is an expectation
A likelihood answers: if the parameter were this value, how probable would the data we actually saw be? Three heads in a row are much more likely if \(P(\text{heads})=0.9\) (\(0.9^3=0.729\)) than if the coin is fair (\(0.5^3=0.125\)). Training often means raising that likelihood, or equivalently lowering \(-\log\) of it.
Cross-entropy loss for classification is the average of \(-\log p_{\text{model}}(y_i\mid x_i)\) over the batch:
\[
L=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p_{\text{model}}(y_i\mid x_i).
\]
That average is an expectation \(\mathbb{E}[-\log p_{\text{model}}(y\mid x)]\), taken with respect to the data (and, in the limit, the data distribution). A confident, correct prediction makes \(-\log p\) small; a confident wrong one makes it large.
import numpy as np
p_correct = np.array([0.8, 0.3, 0.9])   # model probability of the true class
L = -np.log(p_correct).mean()           # cross-entropy on this tiny batch

title: Linear algebra essentials
text:
Vectors and matrices
A vector is an ordered list of numbers, or an arrow: \(v=(3,4)\) has two components. A matrix is a table of numbers, or several vectors placed side by side (or one under another).
Machine learning spends most of its time doing arithmetic with these objects. A row of data is a vector. A batch of rows is a matrix. The weights of a layer are a matrix.


The dot product
The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up:
\[
(1,2,3)\cdot(0.5, 0.1, 2)=0.5+0.2+6=6.7.
\]
That is already a neuron without the activation: a weighted sum of inputs. In matrix notation people write \(x^\top w\) or \(x\cdot w\).
import numpy as np
np.dot([1, 2, 3], [0.5, 0.1, 2])   # 6.7


Matrix multiplication versus \(\odot\)
Matrix multiplication mixes rows of the first matrix with columns of the second. Element-wise multiplication (\(\odot\)) never mixes: it only pairs the entry with its neighbour in the same place. They are different operations, and both appear in models.
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}19&22\\43&50\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}
\odot
\begin{pmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}5&12\\21&32\end{pmatrix}.
\]
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
A @ B    # matrix product: [[19, 22], [43, 50]]
A * B    # element-wise:    [[ 5, 12], [21, 32]]


Transpose and norms
The transpose \(A^\top\) flips rows and columns. It is how you turn a column into a row, or line up shapes so a product is legal.
A norm \(\lVert v\rVert\) answers “how big is this vector?”. The L2 norm \(\lVert v\rVert_2=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+\cdots}\) is ordinary length. The squared L2 norm \(\lVert v\rVert_2^2\) is what you usually put in a loss, for example each term of k-means inertia.
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
A.T                      # [[1, 3], [2, 4]]
np.linalg.norm([3, 4])   # 5.0


Why machine learning is matrix multiplication
One dense layer, on one input, is “multiply, add a bias, then activate”:
\[
y = f(xW+b).
\]
A whole mini-batch \(X\) (rows are examples) is the same product, computed at once: \(Y=f(XW+b)\). That is why GPUs matter, and why shapes (\(n\times d\) times \(d\times k\)) are worth checking twice.
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
W = np.array([[0.2, 0.5],
              [0.1, 0.3],
              [0.4, 0.0]])
x @ W   # two units: [1.6, 1.1]





flowchart TD
  A[Inputs x] --> B[Matrix multiply xW plus bias]
  B --> C[Activation f]
  C --> D[Next layer]






The non-linearity \(f\) is an activation function. The multiply-and-add is the linear algebra on this page.

title: Calculus essentials
text:
A derivative is a slope
If \(y=f(x)\), the derivative \(f'(x)\) (also written \(\frac{dy}{dx}\)) is the slope of \(f\) at \(x\): how fast \(y\) rises or falls if \(x\) moves a little.
A straight line \(y=3x+1\) has slope \(3\) everywhere. A curve \(y=x^2\) has slope \(2x\): at \(x=2\) the slope is \(4\), at \(x=0\) it is flat.
For a picture of a steep slope versus a gentle one, see the gradient primer on the activation-functions page.


Partial derivatives and the gradient \(\nabla\)
When a function has several inputs, a partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\) asks: how fast does \(f\) change if I move only \(x\), and hold the other inputs still?
The gradient \(\nabla f\) is the vector of all those partials. It points in the direction of steepest increase. To reduce a loss, we step the other way.
A tiny example. \(f(x,y)=x^2+3y\) at \((2,1)\): \(\partial f/\partial x=4\), \(\partial f/\partial y=3\), so \(\nabla f=(4,3)\).


The chain rule, which backpropagation rests on
If a value is a function of a function, \(y=f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\), the slopes multiply:
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\cdot g'(x).
\]
A tiny example. \(y=(2x+1)^2\). Let \(u=2x+1\). Then \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2u\cdot 2=4(2x+1)\). At \(x=1\), the slope is \(12\).
A neural network is a long chain: input, then \(xW+b\), then an activation, then the next layer, then a loss. Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to that chain, from the loss back to each weight. If an activation has a tiny slope, the product shrinks; that is the vanishing-gradient story on the activation-functions page.
# y = (2x + 1)**2 at x = 1, numerical check of the slope 12
h = 1e-6
x = 1.0
(((2*(x+h)+1)**2) - ((2*(x-h)+1)**2)) / (2*h)   # about 12


Gradient descent, one step
To reduce a loss \(L(w)\), move against the gradient:
\[
w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\nabla L(w),
\]
where \(\eta\) (the learning rate) is a small positive step size.
A tiny numeric example. Let \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), so \(\nabla L=2(w-3)\). Start at \(w=5\) with \(\eta=0.1\):
\[
w \leftarrow 5 - 0.1\times 4 = 4.6.
\]
The loss goes from \((5-3)^2=4\) to \((4.6-3)^2=2.56\). One more step: \(4.6-0.1\times 3.2=4.28\), and the loss falls again. Repeat until the slope is almost zero (here, at \(w=3\)).
w, lr = 5.0, 0.1
for _ in range(3):
    grad = 2 * (w - 3)
    w = w - lr * grad
    print(w, (w - 3)**2)
# 4.6  2.56
# 4.28 1.6384
# 4.024 1.0486...





flowchart TD
  A[Compute the loss] --> B[Compute the gradient]
  B --> C["Step: w = w minus lr times grad"]
  C --> A

title: A Brief Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
From Biology to Formalization
Introduction, Motivation and History
How to teach a computer? You can either write a rigid program – or you can enable the computer to learn on its own. Living beings don’t have any programmer writing a program for developing their skills, which only has to be executed. They learn by themselves – without the initial experience of external knowledge – and thus can solve problems better than any computer today. KaWhat qualities are needed to achieve such a behavior for devices like computers? Can such cognition be adapted from biology? History, development, decline and resurgence of a wide approach to solve problems.
Biological Neural Networks
How do biological systems solve problems? How is a system of neurons working? How can we understand its functionality? What are different quantities of neurons able to do? Where in the nervous system are information processed? A short biological overview of the complexity of simple elements of neural information processing followed by some thoughts about their simplification in order to technically adapt them.
Components of Artificial Neural Networks
Formal definitions and colloquial explanations of the components that realize the technical adaptations of biological neural networks. Initial descriptions of how to combine these components to a neural network.
How to Train a Neural Network?
Approaches and thoughts of how to teach machines. Should neural networks be corrected? Should they only be encouraged? Or should they even learn without any help? Thoughts about what we want to change during the learning procedure and how we will change it, about the measurement of errors and when we have learned enough.

title: A Brief Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
Supervised learning Network Paradigms
The Perceptron
A classic among the neural networks. If we talk about a neural network, then in the majority of cases we speak about a percepton or a variation of it. Perceptrons are multi-layer networks without recurrence and with fixed input and output layers. Description of a perceptron, its limits and extensions that should avoid the limitations. Derivation of learning procedures and discussion about their problems.
Radial Basis Functions
RBF networks approximate functions by stretching and compressing Gaussians and then summing them spatially shifted. Description of their functions and their learning process. Comparison with multi-layer perceptrons.
Recurrent Multi-layer Perceptrons
Some thoughts about networks with internal states. Learning approaches using such networks, overview of their dynamics.
Hopfield Networks
In a magnetic field, each particle applies a force to any other particle so that all particles adjust their movements in the energetically most favorable way. This natural mechanism is copied to adjust noisy inputs in order to match their real models.
Learning Vector Quantisation
Learning vector quantization is a learning procedure with the aim to reproduce the vector training sets divided in predefined classes as good as possible by using a few representative vectors. If this has been managed, vectors which were unkown until then could easily be assigned to one of these classes.

title: A Brief Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
Unsupervised learning Network Paradigms
Self Organizing Feature Maps
A paradigm of unsupervised learning neural networks, which maps an input space by its fixed topology and thus independently looks for simililarities. Function, learning procedure, variations and neural gas.
Adaptive Resonance Theory
An ART network in its original form shall classify binary input vectors, i.e. to assign them to a 1-out-of-n output. Simultaneously, the so far unclassified patterns shall be recognized and assigned to a new class.

In Grimm’s dictionary the extinct German word “Kluster” is described by “was dicht und dick zusammensitzet (a thick and dense group of sth.)”. In static cluster analysis, the formation of groups within point clouds is explored. Introduction of some procedures, comparison of their advantages and disadvantages. section: Formal vs actual, parameter vs argument
text:
Formal vs actual, parameter vs argument

The terminology around data passed to functions can feel confusing. To make matters worse, some sources refer to what we have called parameters and arguments as formal and actual parameters. Other sources call them formal and actual arguments. The Python documentation specifies only the terms argument and parameter, so that is what we will use as well.

What actually happens when the function call greet("Emily") is executed?
In the function definition greet(name) the parameter name behaves for all intents and purposes just like a normal variable. We can use it within the function just like we have used variables in the many main functions in our programs thus far.
In the function call greet("Emily") the argument “Emily” is just like any other string we have come across before. For example, we can assign it to a variable.
So, when the function call is executed, the value of the argument, “Emily”, is assigned to the parameter variable name. For the duration of this execution of the function, name = “Emily”. When the function is called with a different argument, the value of name will be different. 
This terminology may all seem a bit superfluous, but computer science as a discipline does aim to be as exact a science as possible. Using well defined terminology helps.

title: Python Helsinki: 2
text:
Statement
A statement is a part of the program which executes something. It often, but not always, refers to a single command.
For example, print(“Hi!”) is a statement which prints out a line of text. Likewise, number = 2 is a statement which assigns a value to a variable.
A statement can also be more complicated. It can, for instance, contain other statements. The following statement spans three lines:
if name == "Anna":
    print("Hi!")
    number = 2
In the above case there are two statements (a print statement and an assignment statement) within a conditional statement.

title: Python Helsinki: 2
text:
Block
A block is a group of consecutive statements that are at the same level in the structure of the program. For example, the block of a conditional statement contains those sta
if age > 17:
    # beginning of the conditional block
    print("You are of age!")
    age = age + 1
    print("You are now one year older...")
    # end of the conditional block

print("This here belongs to another block")
In Python blocks are expressed by indenting all code in the block by the same amount of whitespace.

NB: the main block of a Python program must always be at the leftmost edge of the file, without indentation:

# this program will not work because it is not written at the leftmost egde of the file
  print("hello world")
  print("this program is not very good...")

title: Python Helsinki: 2
text:
Expression
An expression is a bit of code that results in a determined data type. When the program is executed, the expression is evaluated so that it has a value that can then be used in the program.
Here are a few examples of expressions:



Expression
Value
Type
Python data type




2 + 4 + 3
9
integer
int


“abc” + “de”
“abcde”
string
str


11 / 2
5.5
floating point number
float


2 * 5 > 9
True
Boolean value
bool



Because all expressions have a type, they can be assigned to variables:
# the variable x is assigned the value of the expression 1 + 2
x = 1 + 2
Simple expressions can be assembled together to form more complicated expressions, for example with arithmetic operations:
# the variable y is assigned the value of the expression '3 times x plus x squared'
y = 3 * x + x**2

title: Python Helsinki: 2
text:
Function

A function executes some functionality. Functions can also take one or more arguments, which are data that can be fed to and processed by the function. Arguments are sometimes also referred to as parameters. There is a technical distinction between an argument and a parameter, but the words are often used interchangeably. For now it should suffice to remember that both terms refer to the idea of some data passed to the function.

A function is executed when it is called. That is, when the function (and its arguments, if any) is mentioned in the code. The following statement calls the print function with the argument “this is an argument”:
print("this is an argument")
Another function you’ve already used often is the input function, which asks the user for input. The argument of this function is the message that is shown to the user:
name = input("Please type in your name: ")
In this case the function also returns a value. After the function has been executed, the section of code where it was called is replaced by the value it returns; it is another expression that has now been evaluated. The function input returns a string value containing whatever the user typed in at the prompt. The value a function returns is often stored in a variable so that it can be used in the program later on.

title: Python Helsinki: 2
text:
Data type
Data type refers to the characteristics of any value present in the program. In the following bit of code the data type of the variable name is string or str, and the data type of the variable result is integer or int:
name = "Anna"
result = 100
You can use the function type to find out the data type of any expression. An example of its use:
print(type("Anna"))
print(type(100))
Sample output
<class 'str'>
<class 'int'>

title: Python Helsinki: 2
section: Alternative branches using the elif statement
text:
Alternative branches using the elif statement
Often there are more than two options the program should account for. For example, the result of a football match could go three ways: home wins, away wins, or there is a tie.
A conditional statement can be added to with an elif branch. It is short for the words “else if”, which means the branch will contain an alternative to the original condition.

Importantly, an elif statement is executed only if none of the preceding branches is executed.








conditional statement can be added to with an elif branch


Let’s have a look at a program which determines the winner of a match:
goals_home = int(input("Home goals scored: "))
goals_away = int(input("Away goals scored: "))

if goals_home > goals_away:
    print("The home team won!")
elif goals_away > goals_home:
    print("The away team won!")
else:
    print("It's a tie!")

title: Python Helsinki: 2
text:
Conditions






Simplified combined conditions



The condition x >= a and x <= b is a very common way of checking whether the number x falls within the range of a to b.
An expression with this structure works the same way in most programming languages.
Python also allows a simplified notation for combining conditions:
a <= x <= b
achieves the same result as the longer version using and.
This shorter notation might be more familiar from mathematics, but it is not very widely used in Python programming, possibly because very few other programming languages have a similar shorthand.

Loops
We have now covered conditional structures in some detail. Another central technique in programming is repetition, or iteration. Together these form the fundamental control structures any programmer must master.

They are called control structures because essentially they allow you to control which lines of code get executed when. While conditional structures allow you to choose between sections of code, iteration structures allow you to repeat sections of code.

They are often called loops because they allow the program to “loop back” to some line that was already executed before. The process of executing one repetition of a loop is also referred to as an iteration of the loop.
from math import sqrt
# Write your solution here

while True:
    number = int(input("Please type in a number: "))
    if number == 0:
        break
    elif number < 0:
        print("Invalid number")
    else:
        print(sqrt(number))
print("Exiting...")
Sample output
Please type in a number: 5
2.23606797749979
Please type in a number: 4
2
Please type in a number: -4
Invalid number
Please type in a number: 0
Exiting...
