title: Python Helsinki: 1
text:
Commenting
Any line beginning with the pound sign #, also known as a hash or a number sign, is a comment. This means that any text on that line following the # symbol will not in any way affect how the program functions. Python will simply ignore it.
Comments are used for explaining how a program works, to both the programmer themselves, and others reading the program code. In this program a comment explains the calculation performed in the code:
print("Hours in a year:")
# there are 365 days in a year and 24 hours in each day
print(365*24)






Choosing a good name for a variable



It is often useful to name variables according to what they are used for.

For example, if the variable contains a word, the name word is a better choice than, say, a.

There is no set limit to the length of a variable name in Python, but there are some other limitations. A variable name should begin with a letter, and it can only contain letters, numbers and underscores _.
Lowercase and uppercase letters are different characters. The variables name, Name and NAME are all different variables. While this rule has a few exceptions, we will ignore those for now.
It is a common programming practice in Python to use only lowercase characters in variable names. If the variable name consists of multiple words, use an underscore between the words. While this rule also has a few exceptions, we will ignore those for now.

title: Python Helsinki: 1
text:
Printing with f-strings
What if we want to have more flexibility and control over what we print out? So called f-strings are another way of formatting printouts in Python. The syntax can initially look a bit confusing, but in the end f-strings are often the simplest way of formatting text.
With f-strings the previous example would look like this:
result = 10 * 25
print(f"The result is {result}")
Let’s break this apart. In the very beginning of the string we are printing out there is the character f. This tells Python that what follows is an f-string. Within the string, enclosed in curly brackets, is the variable name result. The value it contains becomes a part of the printed string. The printout is exactly the same as in the previous examples:
Sample output
The result is 250

title: Python Helsinki: 1
text:
Numbers as input
Usually you do not need to create two separate variables (like input_str and year above) to read a number value from the user. Instead, reading the input with the input function and converting it with the int function can be achieved in one go.
Similarly, a string can be converted into a floating point number with the function float. This programs asks the user for their height and weight, and uses these to calculate their BMI:
year = int(input("Which year were you born? "))
print(f"Your age at the end of the year 2021: {2021 - year}" )

height = float(input("What is your height? "))
weight = float(input("What is your weight? "))

height = height / 100
bmi = weight / height ** 2

print(f"The BMI is {bmi}")
Sample output

Your age at the end of the year 2021: 26

What is your height? 163
What is your weight? 74.45
The BMI is 28.02137829801649

Indentation



Python recognises that a block of code is part of a conditional statement if each line of code in the block is indented the same. That is, there should be a bit of whitespace at the beginning of every line of code within the code block. Each line should have the same amount of whitespace.


a = 3
condition = a < 5
print(condition)
if condition:
    print("a is less than 5")

True

if points < 100:
    points *= 1.1
    print("Your bonus is 10 %")

elif points >= 100:

print("You now have", points, "points")

title: Machine Learning
text:
Introduction
Machine learning (ML) is a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) focused on enabling computers and machines to imitate the way that humans learn, to perform tasks autonomously, and to improve their performance and accuracy through experience and exposure to more data.
UC Berkeley breaks out the learning system of a machine learning algorithm into three main parts.

A Decision Process: In general, machine learning algorithms are used to make a prediction or classification. Based on some input data, which can be labeled or unlabeled, your algorithm will produce an estimate about a pattern in the data.
An Error Function: An error function evaluates the prediction of the model. If there are known examples, an error function can make a comparison to assess the accuracy of the model.
A Model Optimization Process: If the model can fit better to the data points in the training set, then weights are adjusted to reduce the discrepancy between the known example and the model estimate. The algorithm will repeat this iterative “evaluate and optimize” process, updating weights autonomously until a threshold of accuracy has been met.

This same loop, with a single weight and a short program, is on The learning loop.

What is machine learning?


Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence, which is broadly defined as the capability of a machine to imitate intelligent human behavior. Artificial intelligence systems are used to perform complex tasks in a way that is similar to how humans solve problems.



Deep Learning and Machine Learning



From: Optical neural networks: progress and challenges


Neuron structure and artificial neural network. a Structure of biological neurons. b Mathematical inferring process of artificial neurons in multi-layer perceptron, including the input, weights, summation, activation function, and output. c Multi-layer perceptron artificial neural network


Machine Learning fields
The core idea that classifies Deep Learning as a field of Machine Learning (ML) lies in its use of artificial neural networks (ANNs) with multiple layers to automatically learn patterns and representations from data. Unlike traditional ML, which often requires manual feature engineering, deep learning models extract features hierarchically, enabling them to handle complex tasks such as image recognition and natural language processing.
Key fields in Machine Learning:

Supervised Learning
Unsupervised Learning
Semi-Supervised Learning
Reinforcement Learning

Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning, Semi-Supervised Learning, and Reinforcement Learning are key paradigms in machine learning. Each approach addresses different types of problems and data availability.
Supervised learning uses labeled data for training, while unsupervised learning identifies patterns in unlabeled data. Semi-supervised learning combines both, and reinforcement learning focuses on decision-making through trial and error in dynamic environments.











Subfield
Definition
Objective
Examples
Applications




Supervised Learning
Trains a model on a labeled dataset where each training example is paired with an output label.
Learn a mapping from inputs to outputs for predictions on unseen data.
Linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, SVMs
Classification (e.g., spam detection), regression (e.g., house prices)


Unsupervised Learning
Trains a model on data without labeled outputs to learn the underlying structure or distribution of the data.
Identify patterns, groupings, or relationships within the data.
Clustering (e.g., k-means, hierarchical), dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA)
Market segmentation, anomaly detection, exploratory data analysis


Semi-Supervised Learning
Combines both labeled and unlabeled data for training, typically with a small amount of labeled data.
Improve learning accuracy by leveraging additional unlabeled data while benefiting from labeled examples.
Techniques using supervised methods enhanced by clustering.
Scenarios where labeling data is expensive or time-consuming (e.g., image classification)


Reinforcement Learning
Involves training an agent to make decisions by interacting with an environment and learning through trial and error.
Learn a policy that maximizes cumulative rewards over time.
Q-learning, deep reinforcement learning (using neural networks)
Robotics, game playing (e.g., AlphaGo), autonomous systems






Deep Learning as distinct field
Deep learning is indeed considered a distinct field within the broader domain of machine learning.
It is characterized by its use of deep neural networks to learn complex patterns from large datasets.






Deep Learning as a Distinct Field



Core Concept: Deep learning utilizes artificial neural networks with multiple layers (deep architectures) to automatically learn representations from data, distinguishing it from traditional machine learning methods that often rely on manual feature extraction.
Complexity Handling: Deep learning excels at managing high-dimensional data and capturing non-linear relationships, making it particularly effective for tasks like image and speech recognition.



Relationship to Other Machine Learning Subfields
Deep learning can be viewed as a specialized approach within the following main subfields of machine learning, here’s how deep learning fits into the classification of machine learning and its relationship with other fields:

Supervised Learning:

Definition: Involves training models on labeled datasets where the output is known.
Deep Learning Application: Deep learning models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), are frequently used for supervised tasks like classification and regression.

Unsupervised Learning:

Definition: Involves training models on unlabeled data to discover hidden patterns or structures.
Deep Learning Application: Techniques like autoencoders and generative adversarial networks (GANs) are used in deep learning for tasks such as clustering and anomaly detection.

Semi-Supervised Learning:

Definition: Combines both labeled and unlabeled data for training, leveraging the strengths of both approaches.
Deep Learning Application: Deep learning can enhance semi-supervised methods by using pre-trained models to extract features from unlabeled data.

Reinforcement Learning:

Definition: Involves training agents to make decisions by interacting with an environment, receiving feedback in the form of rewards or penalties.
Deep Learning Application: Deep reinforcement learning combines neural networks with reinforcement learning principles, enabling agents to learn complex behaviors in environments with high-dimensional state spaces.



Deep learning represents a significant advancement in machine learning, offering powerful tools for both supervised and unsupervised tasks. Its ability to automatically learn features from raw data sets it apart from traditional machine learning methods, making it a critical area of research and application in modern AI systems.

title: Language model training
text:
Teaching the typist what to expect






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


Training is how the next-token machine gets its instincts. You show it text, ask it to guess the next token, and punish it when it is surprised. Do that at huge scale and you get pretraining. Change the mix of data, or the kind of feedback, and you get the later stages: midtraining, instruction following, preference learning, and — when you can check an answer automatically — reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.






Everyday example



Think of an apprenticeship. First the apprentice reads a vast, messy library (pretraining). Then you put more of the books they will actually need on the desk — the maths, the code, the house style (midtraining). Then you stand next to them and correct how they answer a request (instruction fine-tuning), or you compare two answers and say which you prefer (preference learning). For some jobs you do not need a taste judgement at all: the unit tests pass, or they do not. That last kind of feedback is the one the lecture highlights for agents.


The 2017 paper’s own training setup — WMT data, Adam with a warmup, the BLEU numbers — stays on the reader’s guide to Attention Is All You Need. This page is the modern recipe around that same next-token loss: pretraining, midtraining, post-training, and training for agents.


The loss: next-token cross-entropy
The usual training loss is cross-entropy on the next token. For a vocabulary of size \(V\), with \(y_i = 1\) on the token that actually appeared and \(0\) elsewhere,
\[
L = - \sum_{i=1}^{V} y_i \log p_i,
\]
which is just \(-\log p\) on the correct token. You raise the probability of what was written; everything else is pushed down.







Figure 1: Cross-entropy over the vocabulary: only the token that appeared in the data contributes to the sum — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 100. Lecture original.




The lecture also works a numerical example: if the model assigned probability \(0.0124\) to the next word, it writes \(\mathrm{Loss} = -\log(0.0124) = 1.907\). That arithmetic uses a logarithm base 10. Standard training implementations use the natural log, so the same probability would contribute about \(4.39\) nats, not \(1.907\). The qualitative point is unchanged: a less confident correct token means a larger loss. The \(0.0124\) itself is a teaching number, like the other token probabilities in this lecture.


Pretraining, and the data pipeline
Pretraining is next-token prediction on a huge public mix: web crawls, books, code, and whatever else the recipe allows. The interesting engineering is not the loss — it is the data.
A typical pipeline extracts text from HTML, filters by language and quality, deduplicates, and only then trains. The lecture shows this with DataComp-LM (Li et al., 2024): starting from a Common Crawl pool, a sequence of heuristic filters, deduplication, and model-based quality filters leaves a much smaller training set.







Figure 2: Construction of the DataComp-LM baseline from a Common Crawl pool — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 103. Original: Figure 4 of DataComp-LM (Li et al., 2024).




Other pointers from the lecture are in the same spirit: The Pile (Gao et al., 2020) as a documented mixed corpus; specialised collections such as Nemotron-CC-Math; and Olmix, a 2026 framework for thinking about data mixing across the whole development process, not only at the start.


Midtraining
Midtraining sits between the general pretraining mix and the final post-training stage. The idea is simple: change the data mix so that it leans toward the domains you actually care about — maths, code, and so on — before you start instruction tuning.
The lecture cites two recent arguments for doing this on purpose. The Finetuner’s Fallacy (2026) discusses when it helps to fold target-domain data into the earlier training mix rather than saving it all for fine-tuning. Midtraining Bridges Pretraining and Posttraining Distributions sketches why a stop in the middle can be an easier path, in parameter space, than jumping straight from a general pretrained model to the target.







Figure 3: A schematic of midtraining as a bridge between the pretrained model and the target, instead of a direct fine-tune across a poorly aligned region — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 111. Original: Midtraining Bridges Pretraining and Posttraining Distributions.






Post-training
Post-training is where a pretrained (and perhaps midtrained) model is turned into something that follows instructions and is more pleasant to work with.
Instruction fine-tuning trains on examples of a request and a good response. The lecture’s picture is from Flan (Chung et al., 2022; “Scaling Instruction-Finetuned Language Models”).
Learning from human preferences is the InstructGPT recipe: collect demonstrations and train a supervised policy; collect comparisons and train a reward model; then optimise the policy against that reward model, typically with PPO. The figure is from Ouyang et al., 2022.







Figure 4: The InstructGPT three-step recipe: supervised demonstrations, a reward model from comparisons, then PPO against that reward model — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 114. Original: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022).




Human feedback has well-known cracks, and the lecture lists them (with a nod to CS 329X). Annotators are unreliable. People disagree. The optimisation can learn bad incentives such as sycophancy and a tone of false authority. And the data itself can be sourced unethically. Those are reasons to be careful with preference training, not reasons to skip post-training altogether.


Verifiable rewards, and training for agents
When the task has a checkable answer, you can replace a human preference with a verifier. The lecture calls this reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Typical verifiers are unit tests, a Lean proof checker, exact match, or a system state. The method is a good fit for maths and code, and you still have to be careful about the design of the verifier: models will exploit a sloppy check.
The lecture illustrates the idea with Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) from DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024). That paper is a fair credit for group-relative policy updates and for verifiable maths rewards; “RLVR” as a slogan became common a little later.







Figure 5: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, illustrated with the GRPO loop — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 116. Original: DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024). The lecture uses this figure to explain RLVR; the paper itself introduces GRPO and verifiable maths rewards.




For agents, you also need data that looks like the job. The lecture’s example is SWE-smith (Yang et al., 2025), a recipe for scaling software-engineering agent data rather than hoping general post-training will be enough.


In one table








Stage
What you change
Typical signal




Pretraining
A huge, filtered mix of text
Next-token cross-entropy


Midtraining
The mix, toward the target domains
Still next-token prediction, on a more relevant diet


Instruction fine-tuning
How the model answers a request
Supervised input–output examples


Preference learning (RLHF)
What people prefer, via a reward model
Comparisons, then PPO or a relative of it


RLVR
What a program can check
Unit tests, proofs, exact match, system state


Agent-specific data
Trajectories that look like the product
For example, SWE-smith for software agents





FAQ
Is midtraining just more pretraining? It is the same loss, pointed at a different mix. The claim in the papers the lecture cites is that this bridge can matter more than people expect if they save all of the domain data for a short fine-tune at the end.
Why not always use human preferences? Because annotators disagree, the reward model can be gamed, and the process can teach sycophancy. Where a verifier exists, it is often a cleaner training signal — if you design the verifier honestly.
Does a passing unit test mean the agent is right? It means it passed the tests you wrote. A weak test suite is a reward the model can hack. The lecture’s warning about verifier design is the important part.
Where does this meet inference? Training decides what the model can do. Inference decides how much compute you spend when it is already trained — including the test-time scaling that has started to look a little like extra training, done at read time.

title: Language model architecture
text:
The shape of the typist






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


Once you know that a language model is a next-token distribution, the next question is what computes it. The architecture is the typist’s memory: how much of the past they can see, how much that look-back costs, and what they have to throw away to go faster.
This page follows the lecture’s short history, then the Transformer, then linear attention and the hybrid designs that try to keep both.






Everyday example



Think of reading a long letter. Full attention is like being able to glance back at every earlier sentence whenever you need it: accurate, and slower as the letter grows. A recurrent model is like keeping only a short mental note of what has been said; cheap, and easy to forget a name from page one. Linear attention is a compressed notebook of constant size: you can keep writing for a long time without the notebook getting thicker, but the notes are a summary, not the original pages. A lot of current systems keep a few “glance back at everything” pages and use the notebook for the rest.




A brief history
The lecture’s sketch is short on purpose:

N-gram models (the standard toolkit well into the 2000s, and in use long before) guess the next word from a fixed window of previous words. They are simple, and they hit a wall: a slightly longer phrase, or a slightly new wording, and the table has never seen it.
The first widely cited neural language model is Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent and Jauvin, A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (JMLR, 2003). Words become vectors; a network shares parameters across contexts instead of storing a giant sparse table.
Recurrent neural language models, associated in the lecture with work around 2010 (Mikolov and colleagues), fold the past into a hidden state that is updated token by token.
Long short-term memory was introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997. The lecture’s phrase is that it was popularised for language models in 2014 — a fair mid-2010s date for the wave of LSTM language models and sequence-to-sequence work, not the date the cell was invented.

Then the field changed shape.


Transformers
The leap from recurrence to self-attention is already told in two places on this wiki. The evolution of attention is the history: Bahdanau, Luong, then the 2017 decision to drop the recurrent backbone. Attention Is All You Need is the reader’s guide to that paper — encoder and decoder stacks, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, masking, and positional encoding — with the original Figure 1. Transformer by hand works through one block with small integers.
What the lecture adds, for a builder, is the shape you actually meet today. The original paper is an encoder–decoder model for translation. Almost every chatbot you meet is a decoder-only Transformer: embeddings, positional information, blocks of masked self-attention and a feed-forward network, then a softmax over the vocabulary. The paper’s own comparison (Table 1, below) is why that look-back beat recurrence: a shorter path between distant tokens, and more work that can run in parallel, at quadratic cost in the length of the sequence.







Figure 1: Table 1 from the 2017 paper: self-attention has a shorter path length than recurrence and convolutions, at quadratic cost in sequence length — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 61. Original: Table 1 of Vaswani et al. (2017).






Linear attention
Softmax attention is \(O(n^2)\) in the context length, and the KV cache grows with \(n\). That is a tax every agent pays when the transcript, the tools, and the files pile up. The quadratic bill, and the 2020 reformulation that attacks it, are in The evolution of attention: Katharopoulos, Vyas, Pappas and Fleuret rewrite attention with a kernel feature map so the cost can grow as \(O(n)\), with a constant-size state — a different computation, not a faster softmax. FlashAttention, on the same page, is a third idea: keep the original softmax maths, but run it with fewer trips to GPU memory.
The lecture’s comparison is the one to keep for builders:







Figure 2: Full softmax attention versus linear attention: quadratic look-back and a growing KV cache, against a linear scan over a compressed state — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 87. Lecture original.









flowchart TD
  X["Tokens in a long context"] --> S["Softmax attention"]
  X --> L["Linear attention"]
  S --> S1["Each new token can look at every earlier token"]
  S --> S2["Time and KV memory grow with n squared and n"]
  L --> L1["Each new token updates a compressed state"]
  L --> L2["Time is linear; memory can stay constant"]
  S1 --> H["Many systems use both"]
  L1 --> H






The gain is speed and memory. The cost, which the lecture shows with RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), is long-context quality: a compressed state is a worse look-back than attending to the original tokens. A useful side note from the lecture: neither the Transformer nor linear attention forces a hard context limit by itself. What usually caps you is how the model was trained to use its positional embeddings. In practice you are limited to the context length the model learned.


Mixing the two
So people mix them. Some layers, or some heads, keep global softmax attention; the rest use a linear or similarly cheap recurrence. The lecture illustrates this with figures credited to Songlin Yang, DeltaNet Explained (Part III) — the same line of work that sits behind flash-linear-attention — and with a recent hybrid, Kimi K3 (Moonshot, 2026).







Figure 3: Kimi K3 as an example of mixed global and linear attention — CS 329Z Lecture 2 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 90. Original: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence.






Why this matters for agents
The lecture closes the architecture section with a builder’s list, not a theorist’s:

Agents meet extremely long contexts.
Inference efficiency is a design choice, not a later optimisation.
Knowing the architecture helps you pick a model whose memory and attention pattern fit the job.
The harness around the model should play to its strengths and cover its weaknesses. That is the job of an agent engineer, and it is the subject of LLMs for agents.



In one table








Architecture
What it keeps of the past
Cost of a longer context




N-gram
A fixed window of previous tokens
Tables blow up; unseen phrases get no help


RNN / LSTM
A hidden state, updated token by token
Cheap per step; information has to survive the state


Softmax Transformer
Every earlier token, via the KV cache
Time \(O(n^2)\), memory \(O(n)\)


Linear attention
A compressed, often constant-size state
Time \(O(n)\); weaker long-context recall


Hybrid (e.g. mixed global + linear)
A few full look-backs, plus a cheap state
A compromise, now common in practice





FAQ
Why did Transformers replace LSTMs for language models? Training can be parallel across the sequence, and the path from a token far back is short. That tradeoff is Table 1 below, and it is unpacked in The evolution of attention and in the reader’s guide to the 2017 paper.
If linear attention is faster, why keep softmax attention at all? Because the cheap state is a summary. Benchmarks such as RULER show that long-context work still benefits from being able to look at the original tokens. Hybrids are an attempt to have both.
Is the context window a law of the architecture? Not in the strict sense the lecture is careful about. Attention does not forbid a longer sequence. What usually binds you is the positional scheme the model was trained with, plus the memory bill of the KV cache.
Where should I go for the attention equations? The lecture walks through queries, keys, values, the causal mask, and multi-head attention. We unpack the same maths in Attention Is All You Need. This page stays with the design choices that leak into agents.

title: Generative adversarial networks
text:
A generative adversarial network is not one model. It is two, trained against each other.
The generator starts from random noise and tries to make a sample that looks as if it came from the real data. The discriminator looks at a sample and tries to say whether it is real or fake. Each time the discriminator is right, the generator has to do better. Each time the generator fools it, the discriminator has to look more carefully. Both improve by competing.
That idea was introduced in Generative Adversarial Nets (Goodfellow, Pouget-Abadie, Mirza, Xu, Warde-Farley, Ozair, Courville and Bengio, 2014). The paper appeared at NIPS 2014; the proceedings PDF is the published version, and the arXiv PDF is 1406.2661.
The Generative AI overview already has a short GAN panel. This page is the walk-through: the analogy, the two players, the minimax objective, the training loop, a tiny live example, the usual failure modes, and the line of famous variants.

title: Generative adversarial networks
section: Is a GAN one neural network?
text:
Is a GAN one neural network?
No. It is two, with opposite jobs, updated in turn. The object you sample from after training is the generator. The discriminator is the teacher (and the critic) that made that generator useful.

title: Generative adversarial networks
text:
Why start from noise \(z\)?
If \(G\) had no random input, it could only produce one sample. The noise is the blank paper in the back room: different \(z\) should become different fakes, so that \(G\) covers the distribution rather than a single point.

title: Generative adversarial networks
section: How do we know the game has ended?
text:
How do we know the game has ended?
In the theory of the 2014 paper, the game is won when \(G\) has recovered \(p_{\text{data}}\) and \(D\) outputs \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) on every sample. In practice you never see that clean ending. You look at samples, and at whether \(D\) is still learning, and you stop when the fakes are good enough — or when the training has collapsed.

title: Generative adversarial networks
section: Why is mode collapse so common?
text:
Why is mode collapse so common?
Because the generator is rewarded for fooling the discriminator, not for covering every mode of the data. One very good fake can be a local win, and then \(G\) has little reason to explore. That is why later work (feature matching, unrolling, the Wasserstein cost) tried to give \(G\) a richer training signal.

title: Generative adversarial networks
text:
Did diffusion make GANs obsolete?
Not entirely. For still-image generation, diffusion models took the lead after 2021. GANs remain part of the toolkit — they are fast to sample from, once trained, and the adversarial idea still appears inside other systems. The right picture is a change of default, not a disappearance.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin, 2017) is the paper that introduced the Transformer. This page is a reader’s guide: what problem it solved, how the architecture is put together, what the experiments showed, and how to walk through the sections without getting lost.
The PDF is on arXiv (1706.03762). It also appeared at NeurIPS 2017; the official proceedings PDF is the one linked from our resources.
The story that leads to the paper — Bahdanau, Luong, then self-attention as the foundation — is in The evolution of attention. A tiny block, worked with integers you can add by hand, is in Transformer by hand. Here we stay close to the paper itself.







Figure 1: The Transformer, model architecture (Figure 1 in Vaswani et al., 2017)

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Encoder and decoder stacks
Each encoder layer has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network. Around each sub-layer the paper puts a residual connection, then layer normalisation:
\[
\operatorname{LayerNorm}\bigl(x + \operatorname{Sublayer}(x)\bigr)
\]
The residual is a skip: the original \(x\) is added back, so the sub-layer only has to learn a change, not the whole signal again.
Each decoder layer has three sub-layers. The first is masked self-attention over the tokens written so far. The second is encoder-decoder attention: the decoder asks questions, and the answers come from the encoder. The third is the same kind of feed-forward network as in the encoder. Residuals and layer norm wrap each of the three, just as in the encoder.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Scaled dot-product attention
This is the attention formula the paper uses, and the one we unpacked in The evolution of attention:
\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
\]
Queries, keys and values are packed into matrices. The scaling \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) stops the dot products growing with the key size and flattening the softmax. The paper contrasts this with Bahdanau’s additive attention: the scores are similar in spirit, but a dot product is a much better fit for fast matrix multiplication on a GPU.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Multi-head attention
One attention can focus on one kind of relationship. The paper runs \(h\) attentions in parallel — the heads — each with its own learned projections of \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\). The heads are concatenated and projected back to \(d_{\text{model}}\).
In the base model there are \(h = 8\) heads, and each head uses \(d_k = d_v = 64\). Because each head is narrower, the total cost stays close to that of a single full-width head.






Everyday example



A team of readers looks at the same page. One tracks who did what, another tracks what it refers to, another tracks nearby words. Then you put their notes together. That is multi-head attention: several looks, then one combined result.


The Transformer uses this block in three places:

Encoder self-attention. Every source position can look at every source position.
Decoder self-attention, with a mask. Each target position can look only at itself and at earlier target positions, never at the future.
Encoder-decoder attention. Each target position can look at every source position. This is the old “look back at the letter” step, now with the same multi-head machinery.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Masking
The decoder must not cheat. When it predicts token \(i\), it may use only tokens before \(i\). The paper enforces that inside attention: illegal scores are set to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, so their weights become zero. The output embeddings are also shifted by one position. Together, those two devices keep the decoder auto-regressive: it writes one token, adds it to the context, and writes the next.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Positional encoding
Because the model reads all the tokens at once, it does not naturally know the order. The paper adds a positional encoding to the embeddings at the foot of both stacks, with the same width \(d_{\text{model}}\), so the two can be summed.
The version they use is a fixed pattern of sines and cosines:
\[
\begin{aligned}
PE_{(pos, 2i)} &= \sin\bigl(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\bigr) \\
PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} &= \cos\bigl(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\]
Even dimensions get a sine, odd dimensions a cosine, and the wavelengths form a geometric progression. They also tried learned positional embeddings and found nearly the same quality (Table 3, row (E)). They kept the sinusoids because the pattern may extend to lengths the model did not see in training.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Feed-forward, residuals and layer norm
The feed-forward network is the same idea as in Transformer by hand: two linear maps with a ReLU in between, applied to each position with the same weights.
\[
\operatorname{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2
\]
In the base model the inner width is \(d_{ff} = 2048\). The recipe is shared across positions, but not across layers: each layer has its own \(W_1\) and \(W_2\).
The residual plus layer norm around every sub-layer is what keeps a stack of six (or more) trainable. You can think of the skip as a handrail: the main signal can still get through if a sub-layer does something awkward.

title: Attention Is All You Need
section: Does a Transformer write the whole translation in parallel?
text:
Does a Transformer write the whole translation in parallel?
No. It can read the source in parallel, and training can exploit that. While writing, it still predicts one token at a time, adds that token to the context, and predicts again. The mask is there to keep that rule.

title: Attention Is All You Need
section: Is the Transformer only an encoder-decoder?
text:
Is the Transformer only an encoder-decoder?
The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder, because it was built for translation. Later work often uses only the decoder (as in GPT-style models) or only the encoder (as in BERT-style models). The blocks inside are the same family.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)?
Without the scaling, the dot products tend to grow with the size of the key, and softmax becomes a sharp spike that is hard to train. Section 3.2.1 of the paper, and the everyday version in The evolution of attention, both start from that observation.

title: Attention Is All You Need
text:
Did they invent attention?
No. Attention, including the encoder-decoder kind, was already in use. The paper’s claim is that attention is enough: you can drop the recurrent backbone and still get a better, more parallel model. That is the “all you need”.

title: Attention Is All You Need
section: The English-to-French BLEU is 41.8 in the table. Why does §6.1 say 41.0?
text:
The English-to-French BLEU is 41.8 in the table. Why does §6.1 say 41.0?
The abstract and Table 2 report 41.8. The paragraph in §6.1 writes 41.0. We have not tried to decide which line is the intended one; when we quote a headline figure we follow the table and the abstract, and we note the prose here so you can see both when you read the paper.

Comparison of three categories of generative models.




Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)

Variational AutoEncoders (VAEs) is a type of autoencoder that extends the basic architecture to learn a probabilistic model of the data.

This allows them to generate new data similar to the original input but not identical.
The key innovation in VAEs is the introduction of a regularization term known as the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, which encourages the learned distribution to match a prior distribution, typically a standard normal distribution.
This regularization term allows VAEs to generate more diverse and realistic data than traditional autoencoders.



Illustration of variational autoencoder model



From Autoencoder to Beta-VAE



Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) were introduced by Ian Goodfellow in 2014. They are a class of generative models that use two neural networks, a generator, and a discriminator, to generate new data.

The generator network takes a random noise vector as input and generates a sample from the data distribution. The discriminator network takes a sample from the data distribution and a sample from the generator network and tries to distinguish between them.

The generator network is trained to fool the discriminator network, while the discriminator network is trained to distinguish between real and fake samples.

It is a neural network architecture that uses attention mechanisms to process data sequences.

title: Deep Learning
text:
Deep learning is a transformative subset of machine learning that utilizes artificial neural networks (ANNs) to model complex patterns in data, inspired by the human brain’s architecture.
Characterized by its ability to process vast amounts of information through multiple interconnected layers, deep learning has driven significant advancements in various fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and automation.[1][2]






In this section



Start with the ANN overview and the chapter on activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh and GELU). Those pages sit just before this introduction in the Deep Learning sidebar.




The rise of deep learning has enabled machines to achieve performance levels that surpass human capabilities in tasks such as image recognition and language translation, marking a pivotal shift in how artificial intelligence (AI) is applied across industries.[1]
Notably, deep learning models, particularly deep neural networks (DNNs), have demonstrated remarkable success in diverse applications, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image analysis and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for sequential data tasks.[3][4]
However, the technology is not without its challenges; issues related to data quality, the demand for skilled professionals, and the interpretability of complex models pose significant hurdles for practitioners and organizations aiming to leverage deep learning effectively.[5][6]
Moreover, ethical concerns regarding bias and transparency in AI decision-making processes have sparked ongoing debates about the responsible development and deployment of deep learning technologies.[7][8]







AI fields


As industries increasingly rely on deep learning to enhance efficiency and innovation, understanding its foundational principles, capabilities, and limitations has become essential. The architecture of deep learning models involves intricate design choices, including layer composition and training algorithms like backpropagation, which are crucial for optimizing performance.[2][9]

With continuous research and development, the field of deep learning is poised for further growth, presenting both opportunities and challenges that must be addressed to harness its full potential in a responsible manner.



Deep learning encompasses various types of models designed to address different types of data and tasks. Each model type has its unique architecture and application area, making them suitable for specific use cases.







A comparative view of AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI (source [16]).



A comparative view of AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI (source [16]).

Deep Neural Networks and Generative AI
Deep neural networks (DNNs) extend traditional neural networks by adding multiple hidden layers, which allows them to learn more complex patterns within the data. As of 2017, DNNs typically contained thousands to millions of units and connections, enabling them to perform tasks such as image recognition and natural language processing at levels that can surpass human capabilities[1]
Each layer in a DNN builds on the previous one, allowing the model to capture intricate patterns through its architecture, which can involve convolutional layers for spatial data processing, pooling layers for dimensionality reduction, and fully connected layers for final classification tasks[9][2]

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) consist of two neural networks: a generator and a discriminator, which are trained simultaneously in a competitive framework.

The generator aims to create realistic synthetic data, while the discriminator evaluates the authenticity of the generated data against real data samples.
This adversarial training process helps improve the quality of generated outputs, making GANs popular in applications such as image generation, video creation, and data augmentation. Their ability to produce high-quality visuals has significantly impacted fields like art, entertainment, and gaming[11][12].

Transformer Models: Transformer models have gained prominence in natural language processing tasks due to their efficiency in handling sequential data without relying on recurrence.

Transformers utilize self-attention mechanisms to weigh the influence of different words in a sentence, allowing for a better understanding of context and relationships within the text.
This architecture has led to significant advancements in machine translation, text summarization, and conversational AI applications, making Transformers a crucial development in the deep learning landscape[3]. The path from the earlier attention models to self-attention, and then to cheaper exact attention, is told in The evolution of attention.

title: ANN: Activation functions
text:
What an activation function is
An activation function is a simple rule that sits at the end of a neuron: after the neuron has formed a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, the activation decides what number is sent on to the next layer.
Without it, a neuron would only ever pass along a straight-line combination of its inputs. With it, the neuron can turn off, saturate, or bend — and that is what lets a network learn curves, not just lines.





flowchart TD
  A[Inputs] --> B[Weighted sum plus bias]
  B --> C[Activation]
  C --> D[Next layer]








Why the network needs non-linearity
If every layer used only a linear map, stacking ten layers would still be one linear map. A composition of straight lines is another straight line, so the whole network could be replaced by a single layer.
A non-linear activation breaks that collapse. Each layer can now fold the space a little, and depth starts to matter. That is why ReLU, sigmoid, tanh and GELU are not decorations: they are what make a deep network actually deep.


The four, in brief
Four functions cover most of what you will meet in class and in modern models. A one-line formula and a one-line intuition for each; the details come after a short word on gradients.








Function
Formula
Intuition




ReLU
\(\max(0,x)\)
Keep the positive part; silence the rest.


Sigmoid
\(1/(1+e^{-x})\)
Squash every input into \((0,1)\).


Tanh
\(\tanh(x)\)
Squash into \((-1,1)\), centred on zero.


GELU
\(x\cdot\Phi(x)\)
A smooth ReLU that lets a little of the negative side through.











The four activations on the left, and their derivatives on the right.











The four activations on the left, and their derivatives on the right.





A gradient primer
Training moves the weights by following a gradient: the slope of the loss with respect to each weight. A handy picture is a ball on a hill. Where the hillside is steep, the slope is large and the ball rolls fast. Where the hillside is almost flat, the slope is small and the ball barely moves. For the symbol \(\nabla\) itself, and a one-step numeric descent, see ML math symbols and Calculus essentials.








A hill with a steep tangent on one side and a gentle tangent on the other. The gradient is that slope.











A hill with a steep tangent on one side and a gentle tangent on the other. The gradient is that slope.



Two practical words will keep coming back:

Cheap. Some activations are a comparison and a max (ReLU). Others need an exponential or a Gaussian CDF (sigmoid, tanh, GELU). In a big network that function is called billions of times, so a cheap slope matters.
Does not shrink. During backpropagation the incoming gradient is multiplied by the slope of the activation. If that slope is \(1\), the signal keeps its size. If the slope is \(0.2\) or \(0.01\), the signal shrinks at every layer and can vanish. If the slope is \(0\), that neuron contributes nothing to the update.



A. ReLU
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x).
\]
A negative input becomes \(0\). A positive input passes through unchanged. The gradient is \(0\) for \(x<0\) and \(1\) for \(x>0\) (the kink at \(0\) is usually given gradient \(0\)).
That is why ReLU is cheap and, for positive inputs, does not shrink the gradient. It is the default hidden activation in convolutional networks and ordinary MLPs, and a solid first choice for an MNIST classifier.
The weakness is dead neurons. If a unit is pushed into the negative side and stays there, it outputs \(0\) and its gradient is \(0\), so the weights that feed it stop receiving updates. A high learning rate, or a bad initialisation, can kill many units this way.








ReLU on top, and its 0-or-1 gradient underneath.











ReLU on top, and its 0-or-1 gradient underneath.





B. GELU
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)=x\cdot\Phi(x),
\]
where \(\Phi\) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal. A widely used approximation is[1]
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)\;\approx\;x\cdot\sigma(1.702\,x),
\]
with \(\sigma\) the sigmoid.
GELU is a smooth ReLU. Around zero it has a small negative dip (the minimum is about \(-0.17\)), then it rises almost like a straight line. The gradient is smooth, and neurons rarely die, because a slightly negative input is not hard-zeroed.
It is the standard hidden activation in Transformers such as BERT and GPT[1][3].
SiLU / Swish, \(x\cdot\sigma(x)\), looks almost identical, but its negative dip is deeper: \(\operatorname{SiLU}(-1)\approx-0.269\), against \(\operatorname{GELU}(-1)\approx-0.159\).


C. Sigmoid
\[
\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.
\]
The range is \((0,1)\), and \(\sigma(0)=0.5\). The derivative is \(\sigma(x)\bigl(1-\sigma(x)\bigr)\), whose maximum is \(0.25\) at \(x=0\). Away from zero the curve flattens, the slope goes toward \(0\), and gradients vanish.
That is why sigmoid is a poor default in hidden layers of a deep net, but it is still the right tool when you need a number in \((0,1)\): a binary output, or a gate in an LSTM.


D. Tanh
\[
\tanh(x)=\frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}.
\]
The range is \((-1,1)\), and the output is zero-centred, which is often a kinder hidden representation than a sigmoid that only sits in \((0,1)\). The derivative is \(1-\tanh^{2}(x)\), whose maximum is \(1\) at the origin — four times the peak sigmoid slope — but tanh still saturates in the tails, so gradients can vanish there too.
It is a classic choice in RNNs and LSTMs, and whenever you want a bounded, signed output. It is not a new shape: it is a rescaled sigmoid,
\[
\tanh(x)=2\sigma(2x)-1.
\]


Why language models moved from ReLU to GELU
Compare a single negative input:
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(-1)=0,\qquad\operatorname{GELU}(-1)\approx-0.159.
\]
ReLU applies a hard cutoff. GELU lets a little of that negative signal through, and the transition is smooth, so the gradient does not jump from \(1\) to \(0\).
GELU was introduced by Hendrycks and Gimpel in 2016[1] and then adopted in BERT and in the GPT family[3]. The catch is important: GELU is not universally better. Its popularity comes from empirical results, not from a theorem that it must win on every task. On a small CNN, ReLU is still often the simpler and faster default.
Later work went a step further. Shazeer (2020) showed that gated linear units, including SwiGLU (a gated SiLU), can improve Transformers[2]. Many later language models use that gated family rather than a plain GELU.


Quiz: Guess the activation function
Four unlabelled curves. Name each one before you open the answers.








Four unlabelled plots, A to D. Guess which activation is which.











Four unlabelled plots, A to D. Guess which activation is which.









Answers






A — ReLU. A hard corner at zero, then a straight line for \(x>0\).
B — GELU. Smooth, almost like ReLU, with a small negative dip.
C — Sigmoid. An S-curve in \((0,1)\), with \(\sigma(0)=0.5\).
D — Tanh. An S-curve in \((-1,1)\), zero-centred.






Python lab
A short numpy and matplotlib walk-through: plot the four functions and their derivatives. Run the cell in a notebook; this page does not execute it at build time.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from math import erf, exp, sqrt, pi

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 800)

def relu(x):
    return np.maximum(0, x)

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

def tanh(x):
    return np.tanh(x)

def gelu(x):
    # exact GELU: x * Phi(x), with Phi the standard normal CDF
    Phi = np.vectorize(lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2))))
    return x * Phi(x)

def relu_grad(x):
    return (x > 0).astype(float)

def sigmoid_grad(x):
    s = sigmoid(x)
    return s * (1 - s)

def tanh_grad(x):
    t = np.tanh(x)
    return 1 - t**2

def gelu_grad(x):
    Phi = np.vectorize(lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2))))
    phi = np.exp(-0.5 * x**2) / sqrt(2 * pi)
    return Phi(x) + x * phi

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

axes[0].plot(x, relu(x), label="ReLU")
axes[0].plot(x, gelu(x), label="GELU")
axes[0].plot(x, sigmoid(x), label="Sigmoid")
axes[0].plot(x, tanh(x), label="Tanh")
axes[0].set_title("The four functions")
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)

axes[1].plot(x, relu_grad(x), label="ReLU'")
axes[1].plot(x, gelu_grad(x), label="GELU'")
axes[1].plot(x, sigmoid_grad(x), label="Sigmoid'")
axes[1].plot(x, tanh_grad(x), label="Tanh'")
axes[1].set_title("Their derivatives")
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Rule of thumb

Hidden layers in a CNN or MLP (for example an MNIST classifier): start with ReLU.
Transformers (BERT, GPT and their relatives): GELU, or a later gated variant such as SwiGLU.
Binary outputs and LSTM gates: sigmoid.
Zero-centred, bounded hidden states (classic RNNs): tanh.

If many ReLU units die, lower the learning rate, or try a smooth alternative such as GELU.

FAQ
Why not use a linear activation in every layer? A stack of linear layers is still one linear layer. You need a non-linearity so that depth can learn curved decision surfaces.
What is a dead ReLU? A neuron that always outputs \(0\). Its gradient is \(0\), so the usual update cannot revive it.
Is GELU always better than ReLU? No. GELU won a lot of language-model bake-offs, but that is an empirical pattern, not a proof. On a small vision model, ReLU is still a good default.
If sigmoid shrinks gradients, why is it still taught? Because it is the natural map into \((0,1)\). Use it at an output, or as a gate, not as the hidden activation of a deep stack.
Is softmax an activation of the same kind? Softmax is a vector normalisation used on a multi-class output. It is not a drop-in hidden activation like the four on this page.
Where does the \(1.702\) in the GELU approximation come from? It is the constant Hendrycks and Gimpel fitted so that \(x\cdot\sigma(1.702x)\) tracks \(x\cdot\Phi(x)\) closely[1].

title: ANN: Mathematical Model
text:
Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias term, and applies an activation function. The output of a neuron can be represented as:
\[
y = f\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b \right)
\]
where ( w_i ) are the weights, ( x_i ) are the inputs, ( b ) is the bias, and ( f ) is the activation function.



From: Optical neural networks: progress and challenges


Neuron structure and artificial neural network. a Structure of biological neurons. b Mathematical inferring process of artificial neurons in multi-layer perceptron, including the input, weights, summation, activation function, and output. c Multi-layer perceptron artificial neural network









Simplified model



A biological neuron consists of three main components: dendrites, soma, and axon[2]. Dendrites receive input signals from other neurons. The soma, or cell body, contains the nucleus and processes information. The axon transmits signals to other neurons through synapses[2][8].

An artificial neuron in a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mimics the biological neuron’s function:

Inputs: Represented as a vector [1] \[x = [x_1, x_2, ..., x_n]\]
Weights: Each input is associated with a weight [1] \[w_i\]
Summation: The neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs:
\[v = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b\]
where \[b\] is the bias term[1].
Activation Function: The sum is passed through an activation function \[f\]
\[y = f(v)\]
Common activation functions include sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent, and ReLU[1][10].

For the four functions in more detail, including GELU, see Activation functions.

Output: The result \[y\] is the neuron’s output[1].

Multi-layer Perceptron Neural Network
An MLP consists of multiple layers of interconnected neurons:

Input Layer: Receives the initial data[3].
Hidden Layers: Process information through weighted connections and activation functions[3].
Output Layer: Produces the final result[3].

The network learns by adjusting weights and biases through backpropagation, minimizing a cost function[4][9]. This process allows the MLP to model complex relationships between inputs and outputs, making it suitable for various machine learning tasks[3][9].

title: Algorithms: e-means
text:
New (Nov 2026)



The paper is fresh and not yet peer reviewed; speedups are as reported by the authors.



Classic k-means, in brief
k-means groups unlabelled points into \(k\) clusters. Lloyd’s algorithm places \(k\) centres, assigns each point to the nearest one, moves each centre to the mean of its points, and repeats. That is the same goal e-means keeps. For the full walk-through — the loop, inertia, k-means++, how to choose \(k\), and a scikit-learn lab — see k-means.
e-means keeps the same \(k\) centroids and the same MSE, but needs far fewer passes over the data. The rest of this page explains what changes, and what the authors report.


Overview
e-means is a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means. It solves the same clustering problem — minimise the mean squared distance of each point to its nearest centroid — but updates those centroids with mini-batch exponential moving averages, so it usually reaches a lower loss in far fewer passes over the data.
It was introduced in November 2026 by Swann Bessa and colleagues at FAIR at Meta and École Nationale des Ponts et Chaussées, and shipped in Faiss 1.16.0[1][2][3].






Same problem, different optimiser



e-means is not a new kind of clustering. The inputs are still the dataset and the number of clusters k. The outputs are still \(k\) centroids and an assignment. What changes is how the centroids move: mini-batches, an exponential moving average, and scaling laws that set the batch size and step size for you[1][3].


The announcement thread, the paper, and the project site (with a browser playground) are the primary sources for this page.


What e-means changes
Think of Lloyd as a teacher who only moves the classroom desks after taking attendance of every student. One complete roll-call, then one simultaneous move.
e-means walks the room in small groups. After each group, every desk slides a little toward the students currently sitting there. The slide is an exponential moving average (EMA): the desk does not jump to the latest group, and it does not forget the groups that came before. It blends the new evidence with what it already knew — like a thermostat that does not slam to the latest reading.
Earlier mini-batch k-means methods (MacQueen, Sculley) already update from small batches instead of the full dataset. They can be faster, but when they have been compared with Lloyd they typically finish at a higher error, and the practitioner has to guess a batch size and a step size[1].







Still from a 2D comparison of Lloyd (full batch) and e-means on the same point clouds.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. A still from the animation in post 3/10: side-by-side Lloyd and e-means, with training MSE against the number of passes.
The authors specialise the EMA rule for a fixed dataset (the usual k-means setting), rather than for a shifting codebook as in VQ-VAEs[1]:

Automatic batch size and step size. Scaling laws, fitted on the DEEP dataset and checked on held-out sets, choose the batch size \(B\) and the initial step \(\alpha_0\) from \(n\), \(k\), and the epoch budget \(T\). You do not run a hyperparameter sweep[1][2].








Diagram of the scaling laws that set batch size and step from n, k and the epoch budget.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 5/10: \(n\), \(k\) and \(T\) go in; batch size \(B\) and step \(\alpha_0\) come out.

A decaying step. The step \(\alpha=1-\gamma\) follows a cosine schedule, from \(\alpha_0\) down to \(0.1\,\alpha_0\), so the centroids settle as training goes on[1].
Dead-cluster revival. If a cluster stops receiving points, e-means periodically splits a busy “donor” cluster into two, following the same idea Faiss uses for Lloyd. The authors report this as the most important ingredient in their ablation[1][2].








Side-by-side 2D clustering with revival off and revival on.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. A still from the bonus animation in post 10/10, comparing dead-cluster revival off and on.

A cheap finalisation. After the last epoch, each centroid is replaced by the exact mean of the points assigned to it in that last pass (the default, which helps training MSE). A slower EMA of the centroids is offered when the goal is out-of-sample (test) MSE[1].

By default e-means starts from a random sample of the data, not from k-means++. The paper finds that k-means++ can shave a little more loss, but its cost is high; for a small epoch budget it is usually better to train a bit longer instead[1].





flowchart TD
  A[Take a mini-batch] --> B[Assign nearest centre]
  B --> C[EMA-update counts and sums]
  C --> D[Revive dead clusters]
  D --> A
  C --> E[Last epoch: exact mean]








Results, as reported by the authors
These figures come from the paper and the announcement thread. They are the authors’ own measurements, mostly on embedding datasets, against strong library baselines — not a re-run on this wiki[1][2].



Claim
What the authors report
Source




Epochs to beat Lloyd at 25 iterations
On a wide array of embedding datasets, e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs
Paper abstract[1]


GPU wall-clock
That epoch advantage is reported as 10–45× in the abstract, and as 9.5× to 45.5× versus Flash-KMeans in Table 4 (medians over seeds, up to 1 billion points)
Abstract and Table 4[1]


Quality at a short budget
Three epochs of e-means from random initialisation beat Flash-KMeans at 25 iterations on all eight main setups in Table 5; after five epochs it also stays ahead of Flash-KMeans with greedy k-means++ initialisation
Table 5[1]


Very large scale
On DINO10B (10 billion DINO embeddings), e-means partitions the data into 16 million clusters in 2.5 epochs, with a loss below Lloyd at 25 epochs
Abstract[1]


Coverage
The thread describes evaluation on 26 datasets, from 100k to 10 billion points, with a results map
Thread, post 6/10[2]



The 10× headline is a comparison with state-of-the-art implementations (Faiss on CPU, Flash-KMeans on GPU), not with a naïve Python loop. Swann Bessa made that distinction in the thread[2].







Histograms of train and test MSE: e-means from a random start versus Lloyd with random and k-means++ initialisation.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 4/10: on these embedding datasets, e-means from a random initialisation (blue) often finishes at a lower loss than Lloyd, including Lloyd with greedy k-means++ (green).







Test loss against epochs, and wall-clock time on CPU and GPU.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 7/10, on DEEP with 1 million vectors and 16,384 clusters. The annotated speedups (12.5× fewer epochs, 11.8× CPU, 13.6× GPU) are the authors’ labels on this figure.







Aggregated GPU time against dataset size, with and without IVF assignment.


Figure: Swann Bessa et al., via the X thread. Post 8/10: at billion scale the authors pair e-means with an IVF index for a further wall-clock cut.






A limitation, also from the paper



The scaling laws were tuned for relatively high-dimensional embedding data. The authors say they are not optimal on very low-dimensional and tiny datasets[1]. In Faiss, the defaults already change in that regime: for \(d \le 16\) the “quality” (smaller) batch law is used, and for \(d \le 2\) dead-cluster revival is turned off[3].




How to try it in Faiss
e-means ships in Faiss 1.16.0 as faiss.contrib.e_means. On CPU, faiss-cpu is enough. On GPU, training runs through PyTorch (with optional Triton or CuTe kernels); the data must already be on the GPU[2][3].
The snippet below follows the official Faiss user guide. Default nepochs is 5, which the authors describe as typically enough to beat Lloyd’s loss at convergence[3].
import numpy as np
from faiss.contrib.e_means import NumpyEmeans

x = np.random.rand(200_000, 64).astype("float32")

em = NumpyEmeans(64, 500)          # d=64, k=500; 5 epochs by default
centroids, labels = em.train(x)    # centroids: (500, 64)

x_new = np.random.rand(100_000, 64).astype("float32")
distances, new_labels = em.assign(x_new)
On a GPU, import Emeans and pass a tensor that is already on the device:
import torch
from faiss.contrib.e_means import Emeans

xg = torch.from_numpy(x).cuda().to(torch.bfloat16)
em = Emeans(64, 1024)
centroids, labels = em.train(xg)
labels from train are the assignments from the last training epoch. Because the centroids still moved during that epoch, they are not always each vector’s nearest final centroid. For exact nearest-centroid labels, call assign on the training set as well[3].


When to use it
A good default when you already cluster with Faiss or another high-performance k-means, especially on large embedding sets, IVF codebook training, or any job where 25 Lloyd iterations are the bottleneck[1][2].
Stay with ordinary k-means for tiny or very low-dimensional problems (the laws are not tuned for them), or when you only have scikit-learn and a small dataset where Lloyd is already cheap. e-means is in Faiss, not in scikit-learn. See the k-means lab for that path.
e-means speeds up training of an IVF index. It is not a claim about later search latency once that index is built; the paper discusses the effect on recall in Appendix L[1][2].


Summary









Lloyd k-means
e-means




Objective
Minimise MSE to \(k\) centroids
The same


Update
Full-dataset mean, each epoch
Mini-batch EMA, then a last-epoch mean


Extra knobs beyond \(k\) and epochs
None in the usual Faiss call
None required: batch size and step come from scaling laws


Typical budget in the paper
25 epochs as the Faiss-style reference
1.4–2.6 epochs to pass that reference loss, 5 by default in Faiss


Initialisation in the main experiments
Often k-means++
Random sample of the data


Where it lives
Faiss Kmeans, scikit-learn, and many other libraries
Faiss 1.16.0, faiss.contrib.e_means





FAQ
Is the “e” a new distance or a new cluster shape? No. The “e” is for the exponential moving average used to update the centroids[1][3].
Do I still choose \(k\)? Yes. \(k\) is still the main modelling choice. The batch size and step size are the parts e-means can set for you[1][3].
Why is it faster if each epoch still assigns points to centroids? The assignment work per epoch is comparable to Lloyd. The speed-up comes from needing many fewer epochs (and from specialised kernels that turn that into wall-clock savings)[1].
Can I set the batch size myself? Yes. In Faiss you can pass batch_size or batch_law="quality" / "throughput". If you set only the batch size, \(\alpha_0\) is still taken from the step-size law[3].
Are the last-epoch labels exact? Not necessarily. Use assign when you need each point’s nearest final centroid[3].


References

[1] Swann Bessa, Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze, and Hervé Jégou, e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs), arXiv:2611.09501, 10 November 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501

title: Algorithms: K-Means
text:
Overview
K-Means algorithms classify data into clusters—where K equals the number of clusters. The data points inside of each cluster are homogeneous, and they’re heterogeneous to data points in other clusters.







Clustering is the job of grouping similar points together when nobody has given you the labels in advance.
Think of a market and a mixed pile of fruit. You want \(k\) stalls. You place the stalls, each fruit goes to the nearest stall, then you slide each stall to the middle of its fruit, and you repeat until the stalls barely move. Apples end up with apples and oranges with oranges — even though you never wrote “apple” on a sign.
That procedure is Lloyd’s algorithm, the classic solver for k-means[1].


Lloyd’s loop

Choose \(k\) — how many groups you want. The algorithm does not pick this for you.
Initialise the centres — pick \(k\) starting points in the data. A common choice is k-means++, which spreads the first centres out instead of dropping them all in one corner[2].
Assign — send every point to its nearest centre.
Update — move each centre to the mean (the average position) of the points assigned to it.
Repeat until the assignment stops changing, or you hit a maximum number of passes.






flowchart TD
  A[Choose k] --> B[Place centres]
  B --> C[Assign nearest centre]
  C --> D[Move to the mean]
  D --> E{Still moving?}
  E -->|yes| C
  E -->|no| F[Done]








The objective: inertia, or WCSS
k-means looks for \(k\) centroids that make the clusters as tight as possible. The usual score is the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), also called inertia: the sum of the squared distances from each point to its nearest centre[3]:
\[
J = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2,
\quad a(i)=\arg\min_j\|x_i-c_j\|^2.
\]
The mean squared error (MSE) is the same quantity divided by \(n\). scikit-learn stores inertia as inertia_ after fit. Lower is tighter, but \(J\) always falls as \(k\) grows, so a smaller inertia alone does not mean a better \(k\). Each term \(\lVert x_i-c_{a(i)}\rVert^2\) is a squared L2 norm: how far that point sits from its centre. See ML math symbols and Linear algebra essentials.


k-means++ initialisation
A bad starting set of centres can trap Lloyd in a weak local minimum. k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007) spreads the first centres out: the first centre is chosen at random, and each next one is sampled with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest centre already chosen[2].
It does not remove local minima, and the seeding itself can be slow on very large data, but it is the usual default in scikit-learn and a clear improvement on a purely random start.


Choosing \(k\)
You still have to choose \(k\). Two simple checks:

Elbow. Plot inertia against \(k\). The curve falls quickly at first, then flattens. The “elbow” is a pragmatic guess for \(k\), not a proof.
Silhouette. For each point, compare how close it is to its own cluster versus the next-nearest cluster. The score sits between \(-1\) and \(1\); values near \(1\) mean tight, well-separated groups. Compute the mean silhouette for several \(k\) and prefer a peak.

Neither method is automatic magic. Use them together with what you know about the data.


Limits you should know

You must choose \(k\).
Results are sensitive to initialisation and can stop in a local minimum.
k-means favours compact, roughly spherical clusters of similar size, because each centre is a mean and the distance is Euclidean. Elongated, nested, or very uneven groups can be split badly.
Scale the features. A variable with a huge range will dominate the distances.
Outliers pull the mean, and therefore the centre.
Many iterations may be needed, and each one rereads the whole dataset. One pass compares each of the \(n\) points to all \(k\) centres in \(d\) dimensions, so the work per pass grows with \(n \times k \times d\). Libraries usually cap the number of passes.



Variants

Mini-batch k-means updates the centres from small batches instead of the full dataset. It can be faster on large data, but you have to choose a batch size, and the final error is often a little higher than full-batch Lloyd.
k-medoids uses an actual data point (a medoid) as the centre of each cluster, rather than the mean. That is often more robust to outliers, and it can use other distances than Euclidean.
e-means (2026) keeps the same MSE objective as k-means, but updates centres with mini-batch exponential moving averages and scaling laws that set the batch size and step for you. See e-means.



Python lab
A short scikit-learn walk-through: make a blob dataset, fit k-means, plot the groups, then draw an elbow curve[3].
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X, y_true = make_blobs(
    n_samples=500, centers=4, cluster_std=0.70, random_state=42
)

model = KMeans(n_clusters=4, init="k-means++", n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels = model.fit_predict(X)

plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=labels, s=20)
plt.scatter(

Topic
In brief




Goal
Split unlabelled points into \(k\) tight groups


Loop
Place centres, assign, move each centre to the mean, repeat


Score
Inertia / WCSS (sum of squared distances); MSE is the same quantity divided by \(n\)


Initialisation
k-means++ is the usual default; still a local-minimum method


Choosing \(k\)
Elbow plot of inertia, plus silhouette, plus domain knowledge


Watch out
Scaling, outliers, non-spherical clusters, many full-dataset passes

e-means, when you already use a high-performance k-means





FAQ
Is \(k\) learned from the data? No. You choose \(k\), then the algorithm places the centres.
Does k-means++ always find the global best clustering? No. It is a better start, not a guarantee. Several restarts (n_init in scikit-learn) are still useful.
Why did my features need scaling? Distances are Euclidean. A feature measured in thousands will drown one measured in units, unless you scale them.
When should I try e-means instead? When the dataset is large and many Lloyd passes are the bottleneck. For a small scikit-learn problem, classic k-means is usually enough. See e-means.

title: Algorithms: Introduction
text:
Machine learning algorithms are sets of instructions that enable computers to learn from data, identify patterns, and make predictions without explicit programming.


What you can do with machine learning algorithms
Machine learning algorithms help you answer questions that are too complex to answer through manual analysis.
Use cases for machine learning algorithms typically fall into one of these categories:

Predict a target,
Find unusual data points,
Predict values,
See how values change over time,
Discover similarities,
Classification

These algorithms form the backbone of machine learning systems, allowing machines to improve their performance over time as they process more data.
At their core, machine learning algorithms:

Analyze large amounts of data
Discover patterns and relationships
Make decisions or predictions based on the learned patterns

Machine learning algorithms are typically categorized into three main types:

Supervised Learning: algorithms make predictions based on a set of labeled examples that you provide.

This technique is useful when you know what the outcome should look like.

Unsupervised Learning: the data points aren’t labeled—the algorithm labels them for you by organizing the data or describing its structure.

This technique is useful when you don’t know what the outcome should look like.

Reinforcement Learning: uses algorithms that learn from outcomes and decide which action to take next.

After each action, the algorithm receives feedback that helps it determine whether the choice it made was correct, neutral, or incorrect.
It’s a good technique to use for automated systems that have to make a lot of small decisions without human guidance.
For example, you’re designing an autonomous car, and you want to ensure that it’s obeying the law and keeping people safe. As the car gains experience and a history of reinforcement, it learns how to stay in its lane, go the speed limit, and brake for pedestrians.








Machine learning algorithms



Machine learning algorithms are mathematical models that implement a finite set of unambiguous step-by-step instructions to achieve a specific goal, such as classification, regression, or clustering. They utilize statistical techniques to enable computers to “learn” from data without being explicitly programmed[1].
