title: ML math symbols, explained easy
text:
The core symbols
A short deck of the symbols you will keep seeing. Each card has one question, a figure, an everyday example, a tiny numerical example, and a NumPy line.


\(\nabla\) — gradient
In one line. Which direction should the parameters move to reduce the loss?








Gradient = which way is downhill.











Gradient = which way is downhill.









Everyday example



You are on the top of a hill, and the next step will make you go down. What is the gradient of this step, the direction of this step? This movement is very important. It’s easy.


Analogy. You are standing on a hill in the fog. The gradient points uphill. To reduce the loss, take a step the other way.
A tiny example. Let \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\). At \(w=5\), the slope is \(2(w-3)=4\). A descent step moves left: \(w\leftarrow 5-0.1\times 4=4.6\), closer to \(3\).
w, lr, grad = 5.0, 0.1, 4.0
w = w - lr * grad   # 4.6
Where it shows up. Gradient descent, and every backward pass. The learning loop is that nudge, repeated. See Calculus essentials and the gradient primer.


\(\mathbb{E}\) — expectation
In one line. What is the average value over all possible outcomes, weighted by probability?








Expectation = a weighted average.











Expectation = a weighted average.









Everyday example



If you take the same bus every morning, some days it is early and some days it is late. The expectation is the average time you would see if you did this for many mornings — not any single day. A loss in a model is the same idea: the average error over many examples.


Analogy. The long-run average if you repeated the same random experiment many times. A fair die has expectation \(3.5\), even though \(3.5\) never appears on a face.
A tiny example. Outcomes \(2\), \(4\), \(10\) with probabilities \(0.5\), \(0.25\), \(0.25\): \(\mathbb{E}[x]=2\cdot 0.5+4\cdot 0.25+10\cdot 0.25=4.5\).
import numpy as np
x, p = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 10.0]), np.array([0.5, 0.25, 0.25])
np.dot(x, p)   # 4.5
Where it shows up. A loss is often an expectation — the average error over data. See Probability and statistics.


\(\odot\) — element-wise multiplication
In one line. Multiply corresponding entries, not entire matrices.








⊙ multiplies matching cells; a matrix product mixes rows and columns.











⊙ multiplies matching cells; a matrix product mixes rows and columns.









Everyday example



You have a shopping list and a “how many I already have” list, item by item: apples with apples, milk with milk. You never mix the apple line with the milk line. In a network, a gate does the same: it keeps or kills each number in its own place.


Analogy. Two shopping lists, item by item. You never mix the apple row with the orange row — that mix would be a matrix product.
A tiny example. \((1,2,3)\odot(4,5,6)=(4,10,18)\).
import numpy as np
np.array([1, 2, 3]) * np.array([4, 5, 6])   # [4, 10, 18]
Where it shows up. LSTM gates (forget gate \(\odot\) cell state), attention masks, and any “keep or kill this entry” operation. See Linear algebra essentials.


\(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) — norm
In one line. How big is a vector or an error?








A vector with its L2 length and the L1 taxi path.











A vector with its L2 length and the L1 taxi path.









Everyday example



To the shop, you can cut across the park (the straight path) or walk the street corners like a taxi. Both answer “how far is it?” — one as a straight line, one as the blocks you actually walk. In ML, a norm asks how big a vector or an error is.


Analogy. The length of an arrow. The everyday L2 (Euclidean) norm is the straight-line distance, the same rule as Pythagoras. The L1 norm is the taxi-city walk, along the axes.
A tiny example. For \(v=(3,4)\), \(\lVert v\rVert_2=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\) and \(\lVert v\rVert_1=3+4=7\). A loss often uses the squared L2 norm, \(25\), so the square root can be skipped.
import numpy as np
np.linalg.norm([3.0, 4.0])   # 5.0
Where it shows up. Distance to a cluster centre (k-means inertia), L2 regularisation \(\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2\), and “how large is this error?”. See k-means and Linear algebra essentials.


\(\arg\max\) — argmax
In one line. Which input gives the highest value?








A curve with the peak marked; argmax is the x-position, max is the height.











A curve with the peak marked; argmax is the x-position, max is the height.









Everyday example



The league table shows the scores, but what you care about is which team finished first, not only how many points they got. That “which one?” is argmax. A classifier does the same: it picks the class with the highest score.


Analogy. Not “how high did the class score?”, but “which class won?”.
A tiny example. Scores \((0.1, 0.7, 0.2)\): the maximum is \(0.7\), and \(\arg\max\) is index \(1\) (the second class, counting from \(0\)).
import numpy as np
np.argmax([0.1, 0.7, 0.2])   # 1
Where it shows up. The predicted class in a classifier: take the output scores (or a softmax) and return \(\arg\max\).


A few more that complete the set


\(\Sigma\) — summation
In one line. Add these terms up.








Bars of 1, 2 and 3 stacking into a total of 6.











Bars of 1, 2 and 3 stacking into a total of 6.









Everyday example



At the till, you add every line on the receipt to get the total. Sigma is just that: plus, plus, plus, written small. Almost every loss adds up the errors in the same way.


Analogy. A running total. The sigma sign is a compact “plus, plus, plus”.
A tiny example. \(\sum_{i=1}^{3} i = 1+2+3=6\). A mean is just a sum divided by the count: \((1+2+3)/3=2\).
import numpy as np
np.sum([1, 2, 3])   # 6
Where it shows up. Almost every loss and every mean: inertia, cross-entropy, sum of squared errors.


\(\prod\) — product
In one line. Multiply these terms together.








0.9 times 0.5 times 0.2 equals 0.09.











0.9 times 0.5 times 0.2 equals 0.09.









Everyday example



Three locks on a bike: the bike is free only if lock 1 and lock 2 and lock 3 are open. When the steps are independent, you multiply the chances. That is how a naïve likelihood treats independent clues.


Analogy. A chain of “and”s: the chance that several independent things all happen is the product of their chances.
A tiny example. \(0.9\times 0.5\times 0.2=0.09\).
import numpy as np
np.prod([0.9, 0.5, 0.2])   # 0.09
Where it shows up. The likelihood of independent events, and the “naïve” product inside Naïve Bayes. Long products of probabilities get tiny, which is why we usually take a \(\log\) next.


\(\log\) — logarithm
In one line. Turn a product into a sum, and stretch small probabilities so they are easier to add and to compare.








A product 0.5 × 0.4 becoming log 0.5 + log 0.4, next to the log curve.











A product 0.5 × 0.4 becoming log 0.5 + log 0.4, next to the log curve.









Everyday example



A few small chances in a row — you catch the bus, the shop is open, they still have milk — make a tiny number when you multiply them, hard to read at a glance. A log turns those “times” into “plus”, so you can add them up calmly. That is why training often uses a log-likelihood or a cross-entropy.


Analogy. A translator: “times” becomes “plus”. That is why we talk about log-likelihood instead of multiplying many tiny numbers (which would underflow).
A tiny example. \(\log(0.5\times 0.4)=\log 0.5+\log 0.4=\log 0.20\). NumPy’s np.log is the natural log.
import numpy as np
np.log(0.5) + np.log(0.4)   # same as np.log(0.5 * 0.4)
Where it shows up. Log-likelihood, cross-entropy \(-\log p\), and log-softmax. See Probability and statistics.


\(\partial\) — partial derivative
In one line. How fast does this function change if I move only this input and hold the others still?








A contour with one axis held fixed, and the slope of that slice.











A contour with one axis held fixed, and the slope of that slice.









Everyday example



On a shower, you can turn only the temperature and leave the flow alone. The partial derivative asks: if I move just this knob, how fast does the water change? In a network, each weight is one knob; the gradient is the list of all those answers.


Analogy. A kitchen with two knobs, heat and time. The partial with respect to heat asks: if I turn only the heat, how fast does the cake change?
A tiny example. \(f(x,y)=x^2+3y\). At \((2,1)\), \(\partial f/\partial x=2x=4\) and \(\partial f/\partial y=3\). The gradient is the vector of both: \(\nabla f=(4,3)\).
h = 1e-6
((2+h)**2 + 3*1 - (2**2 + 3*1)) / h   # about 4
Where it shows up. A network has many parameters. The gradient \(\nabla\) is just the list of all these partials. See Calculus essentials.


\(\sigma\) — a letter with two common lives
In one line. Look at the context: \(\sigma\) may be the sigmoid function, or the standard deviation.








Two panels: a sigmoid curve, and a bell curve with the spread marked.











Two panels: a sigmoid curve, and a bell curve with the spread marked.









Everyday example



The same letter has two everyday jobs, so look at the room you are in. As a dimmer, it squashes a signal to something between off and on — that is the sigmoid in a network. As a spread, it is how much your commute time jumps around from day to day — that is the standard deviation.


Analogy. The same nickname for two classmates. In a network diagram, \(\sigma\) usually means “squash this number into \((0,1)\)”. In a statistics paragraph, \(\sigma\) is “how spread out is this data?”.
A tiny example. The sigmoid at \(0\) is \(\sigma(0)=1/(1+e^{0})=0.5\). The standard deviation of \([2,4]\) (population) is \(1\), because the mean is \(3\) and each value sits \(1\) away.
import numpy as np
1 / (1 + np.exp(0))      # sigmoid(0) = 0.5
np.std([2.0, 4.0])       # 1.0  (NumPy's default is the population std)
Where it shows up. Sigmoid activations and LSTM gates (see Activation functions); standard deviation in data summaries and in the normal distribution (see Probability and statistics).


\(^\top\) and the dot product
In one line. \(^\top\) flips rows and columns; the dot product \(u^\top v\) (or \(u\cdot v\)) multiplies matching entries and adds them up.








A 2×2 matrix flipped to its transpose, and two arrows with a projection.











A 2×2 matrix flipped to its transpose, and two arrows with a projection.









Everyday example



Turning a table on its side is a transpose: rows become columns, like flipping a seating plan. The dot product is a shopping moment: price times quantity for each item, then add — your total, and also the weighted sum inside a neuron.


Analogy. Transpose is turning a table on its corner. The dot product is “how much do these two arrows point the same way?” — or, in a neuron, a weighted sum of inputs.
A tiny example. \((1,2)\cdot(3,4)=1\cdot 3+2\cdot 4=11\). The transpose of \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\).
import numpy as np
np.dot([1, 2], [3, 4])          # 11
np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).T    # [[1, 3], [2, 4]]
Where it shows up. Almost every layer: \(x^\top w\), or a batch written as \(Xw\). See Linear algebra essentials.


\(\in\) — belongs to
In one line. Does this object belong to that set?








A point inside a set S, and a point outside.











A point inside a set S, and a point outside.









Everyday example



Is this key on your keyring, or not? Belongs-to is a simple membership check. In ML it is the same idea: this label belongs to the set of classes, this vector belongs to the space of inputs.


Analogy. A membership badge. \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) means “\(x\) is a real vector with \(n\) entries”.
A tiny example. \(3\in\{1,2,3\}\), but \(4\notin\{1,2,3\}\). A paper will write a weight matrix as \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\).
3 in {1, 2, 3}   # True
Where it shows up. Shapes and spaces: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a label \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\).


\(\approx\) and \(\propto\) — approximately, proportional to
In one line. \(\approx\) means “almost equal”; \(\propto\) means “moves in proportion to” (the same shape, maybe a different scale).








A curve hugging an approximation, and two lines that scale together.











A curve hugging an approximation, and two lines that scale together.









Everyday example



The recipe says “about 180 degrees” — that is approximately, close enough. If you double the guests, you double the flour — that is proportional, the same shape at a new scale. Models use both: a handy approximation, or a posterior that follows likelihood times prior.


Analogy. \(\approx\) is a close hug, not a perfect match. \(\propto\) is “when this doubles, that doubles” — a constant factor may still be hiding.
A tiny example. \(\pi\approx 3.14\). In Bayes, the posterior is \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior (the missing piece is the normaliser \(P(\text{data})\)).
import numpy as np
np.isclose(22 / 7, 3.14, atol=0.02)   # True, roughly
# unnormalised posterior:
# posterior_unnorm = likelihood * prior
Where it shows up. Approximations such as \(\operatorname{GELU}(x)\approx x\cdot\sigma(1.702x)\), and Bayes in Probability and statistics.


\(P(A\mid B)\) — conditional probability
In one line. What is the chance of \(A\), given that we already know \(B\)?








Of the emails that contain “prize”, a slice are spam: 16/24.











Of the emails that contain “prize”, a slice are spam: 16/24.









Everyday example



You already know it is raining. Now, what is the chance you will want a coat? That is “given B, what about A?” — you have narrowed the question to the rainy days. A spam filter does the same: given this word, how likely is spam?


Analogy. Of all the emails that contain “prize”, what fraction are spam? You have already narrowed the pile to \(B\).
A tiny example. \(100\) emails, \(20\) of them spam. The word “prize” appears in \(16\) of the spam emails and in \(8\) of the rest, so in \(24\) emails altogether: \(P(\text{spam}\mid\text{prize})=16/24=2/3\).
16 / 24   # 2/3
Where it shows up. Conditioning, Bayes, and Naïve Bayes. The same example is worked on the probability page.


\(\arg\min\) and \(\min\) — the training question
In one line. \(\min\) is the smallest value; \(\arg\min\) is which input gives that smallest value. Training is \(\arg\min\) of the loss.








A loss bowl with the bottom marked: min is 0, argmin is w = 3.











A loss bowl with the bottom marked: min is 0, argmin is w = 3.









Everyday example



You are buying a phone. The lowest price is the min; which phone has that price is the argmin. Training is the same question: which parameters make the error as small as it can be?


Analogy. The lowest point on the hill (\(\min\)) versus “where do I stand to be at the bottom?” (\(\arg\min\)). The twin of \(\arg\max\).
A tiny example. For \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), the minimum value is \(0\) and \(\arg\min_w L(w)=3\). Training writes \(\theta^\star=\arg\min_\theta L(\theta)\).
import numpy as np
ws = np.linspace(0, 6, 7)
ws[np.argmin((ws - 3)**2)]   # 3.0
Where it shows up. Every training loop: find the parameters that minimise the loss. Prediction often uses \(\arg\max\); learning uses \(\arg\min\).


MSE — mean squared error
In one line. How wrong are we, on average? Square every error, then take the mean.
\[
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2
\]
Read it right to left: for each example \(i\), take the prediction \(\hat{y}_i\) minus the real answer \(y_i\), square it, add them all up (\(\Sigma\)) and divide by how many there are (\(\frac{1}{n}\)).








Taxi receipts with w = 1: squared errors 1, 6.25 and 25 average to 10.75.











Taxi receipts with w = 1: squared errors 1, 6.25 and 25 average to 10.75.









Everyday example



You play darts and throw three. Measure how far each dart lands from the bullseye, square each distance, and average. One wild throw far from the centre ruins your score much more than three throws that are a bit off. That number is your MSE: lower is better, and 0 means every dart hit the bullseye.


Analogy. A penalty score. Small misses cost a little, big misses cost a lot, and above or below costs the same.
A tiny example. Taxi receipts 2 km for €3, 5 km for €7.50 and 10 km for €15, with a guess \(w=1\): predictions 2, 5, 10; errors −1, −2.5, −5; squared 1, 6.25, 25; mean \(32.25/3 = 10.75\). With \(w=1.5\) every error is 0, so MSE \(=0\).
km    = [2, 5, 10]
price = [3, 7.5, 15]
w = 1
errors = [w * x - y for x, y in zip(km, price)]
sum(e * e for e in errors) / len(km)   # 10.75
Where it shows up. The loss of linear regression and most regression models; the number gradient descent pushes down in Taxi Lab 1.

title: Lab#FU01-1: Taxi fare, pure Python
text:
📘 Lab#FU01-1: Taxi fare, pure Python
In this lab you will:

Load three taxi receipts.
Guess a price per kilometre, predict, measure the error, and nudge the guess.
Repeat the loop until the guess settles on €1.50 / km.
Plot how the loss falls.

   Code on GitHub

The story starts in The learning loop. Here you run it yourself, in the page. The editor below is live Python in the browser — no install, no libraries for the loop, matplotlib only draws the loss curve. The first load takes a few seconds.
Price = w · kilometres. The true rate on these receipts is €1.50 per kilometre. You do not tell the program that number. It has to find it.

1 Creating the algorithm
The question. A taxi charges by distance. We have three receipts: 2 km cost €3, 5 km cost €7.50 and 10 km cost €15. What does 7 km cost? We don’t know the rate per kilometre, so we let the receipts teach it to us.
# TODO: find the price of a 7 km trip from three receipts
What we know and what we don’t. We know the kilometres (the input) and the prices (the answers). We don’t know the rate, which we call w. Our whole model is one line, price = w · km, and the machine’s only job is to find a good w.
km    = [2, 5, 10]       # what we know: inputs
price = [3, 7.5, 15]     # what we know: answers
# TODO: w is unknown, the thing to learn
A first guess. We have no idea, so we start badly on purpose and watch it improve.
w = 0.0                  # a bad guess on purpose
Predict. With our guess, what would each trip cost? With w = 0, every trip comes out free.
pred = [w * x for x in km]          # [0, 0, 0]
How wrong are we? We compare each prediction with the real receipt. We square the gaps, so a miss above or below counts the same and big misses count more, then average them. That number is the loss, and we want it small.
loss = sum((p - y)**2 for p, y in zip(pred, price)) / len(km)
Which way to move? Every prediction was too low, so w must go up. The gradient tells us which way and how strongly, like feeling the slope of the hill under your feet.
grad = sum(2 * (p - y) * x for p, y, x in zip(pred, price, km)) / len(km)
A small step. We nudge w a little that way. The learning rate is the step size: too small and we crawl, too big and we bounce past the bottom.
lr = 0.01
w = w - lr * grad
Again and again. We predict, measure and nudge, over and over. The loss drops and w creeps towards 1.50.
for step in range(20):
    # predict, measure, find the direction, step
    ...
When to stop. We stop when the loss barely changes, or after a fixed number of steps.
# TODO: stop when loss < 0.0001, or after N steps
Check the answer. w ≈ 1.50, so 7 km costs about €10.50. Nobody told the program the rate; it found the rate from examples. That’s learning.
print(w * 7)             # ≈ 10.5


2 Guess, predict, error, nudge
Three rides: 2 km for €3, 5 km for €7.50, 10 km for €15. Start at \(w = 0\) — every ride is free — and take steps of size \(0.01\).
The gradient of the mean squared error is the average of \(2 \cdot \text{error} \cdot \text{km}\). A nudge is a small step against that gradient:
\[
w \leftarrow w - 0.01 \cdot \nabla L
\]






Try it



Change learning_rate and press Run. Try a smaller rate, or a larger one.








After the first nudge, \(w\) jumps from \(0\) to \(1.29\). After four steps it is already \(1.4994\). By step 6 it has settled on \(1.50\). Nobody programmed the rate.
Loss starts at \(96.75\) — every ride predicted as free — and drops to about zero once \(w\) reaches \(1.50\).






Reading the code: mean_squared_error





This little function answers one question: how wrong is this weight? Let’s run it by hand with weight = 1.

predictions: what we would charge with this weight: 2, 5, 10.
errors: prediction minus real price: −1, −2.5, −5. Negative means we charged too little.
e * e: square each error: 1, 6.25, 25.
sum(...) / len(km): add them (32.25) and divide by the number of rides (3). The loss is 10.75.

Why square? A miss of −5 and a miss of +5 are equally bad, so the sign must go. And squaring makes big misses hurt much more than small ones: missing by 5 costs 25, missing by 1 costs only 1.
In maths it is written:
\[
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (w \cdot x_i - y_i)^2
\]
Same thing as the code: for every ride, predict, subtract the real price, square, then take the average. With weight = 0 you get the 96.75 above; with weight = 1.5 you get 0. See the MSE card, \(\Sigma\) summation and The loss is a landscape.





3 What you should notice
The learning rate \(0.01\) is a gentle pinch. The same loop, with a bad learning rate, can be slow or can blow up — that is in The learning loop and in Optimization essentials.

title: Agent architectures
text:
The skeleton of an agent






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


A modern language-model agent is not “the model”. It is a small machine built around the model.
CS 329Z Lecture 1 draws that machine as five parts: an LLM core, planning and reasoning, memory, tools, and an environment. The environment is the outside world the agent can observe and act on: a desktop, a browser, a repository, a game, a database, a user. The tools are how it acts: retrieval, a calculator, code, search, file operations, a memory read or write. The model sits in the middle. Planning and reasoning are the model’s intermediate generations — the thoughts that update its own state before it commits to an action. Memory is the trace of what has already happened, and whatever was written down so the context window does not have to hold everything.
ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) is the usual picture of the loop: the model writes a thought, then an action, then sees an observation, then thinks again. Lilian Weng’s LLM Powered Autonomous Agents (June 2023) and Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan and Griffiths; often cited as Sumers and Yao, 2024) organise the same pieces in slightly different diagrams. The names vary; the inventory does not.







Figure 1: A ReAct trace mapped onto the parts of an agent — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 29. The trace is from Yao et al., 2022.









flowchart LR
  Env[Environment] -->|observe| Core[LLM core]
  Plan[Planning and reasoning] --- Core
  Mem[Memory] --- Core
  Core --> Tools[Tools]
  Tools -->|act| Env













Figure 2: The lecture’s diagram of an agent’s key components — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 30.











Figure 3: Two standard pictures of a language-model agent — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 31. Left: Weng, LLM Powered Autonomous Agents (2023). Right: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan and Griffiths, 2024).










Everyday example



You are cooking, you taste the pan, and the salt is gone. A reflex would be to stand still, or to grab the first bottle in reach. A more useful response is to think first: the dish should be savoury; soy sauce is in the cupboard on the right; turn, open the cupboard, look again. The thought is not the action. It is an internal step that changes what you do next. That is what reasoning is for in an agent: not a decoration on the transcript, but a way to choose a better act when the mapping from “what I see” to “what I should do” is hard.




Why reason before you act
The lecture puts this in plain terms. For a person, reasoning covers deduction, analogy, planning. For a language model, “reasoning” is an intermediate generation that imitates some of those processes — not all of them, and not with a guarantee. For an agent, those intermediates are internal actions: they update the agent’s state, and only then comes an external act.
That helps in two directions the lecture labels generalisation and alignment. Generalisation: a thought can carry a goal (“this should be savoury”) across a new kitchen, a new cupboard, a new bottle, so the policy is not a brittle lookup from one observation to one action. Alignment: the thought can also be a place to recall a constraint (“don’t use the bottle that isn’t yours”) before the hand moves.







Figure 4: Why a thought between observation and action helps — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 34.




Reasoning without acting is the older idea: chain-of-thought, where the model thinks in text and then answers, still inside its own context. It can help, and it can also hallucinate a confident wrong path, because nothing in the outside world ever contradicts it. ReAct’s point is that acting — searching, running code, reading a file — gives the next thought something real to work with. The lecture notes, following the paper, that combining the two can reduce the kind of hallucination you get from thought alone, and that acting without thought is a weaker baseline than acting with it. We will not recopy the paper’s tables; the idea is the loop, not a particular score.







Figure 5: A ReAct trace: the model searches, reads, and only then answers — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 36. Example from Yao et al., 2022.




Two close cousins are worth knowing by name:

Self-Consistency (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) samples several reasoning paths and keeps the answer they agree on most. Diversity, then a vote.
Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) lets an agent write a short verbal reflection after feedback, and store that text as a hint for later attempts. A long failed trajectory is distilled into something the next try can actually use.

When several models (or several roles) argue and revise, you get multi-agent debate — the lecture points to Du et al., 2023. When one controller assigns work to specialists, you get an orchestrator. Magentic-One (Microsoft Research) is the example on the slide: a generalist multi-agent system in which an orchestrator coordinates others to solve a complex task. Multi-agent design is a scaling of the same architecture, not a different species. It also creates new failure modes, which we take up under Key challenges.


Memory, because the window is not a life
The context window cannot hold every event an agent will see. Even if it could, attending to the relevant events, or digesting them, would still be hard. So agents need a memory that sits beside the prompt.







Figure 6: A memory stream between perceiving and acting — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 45. The lecture labels this Park et al., 2025; the diagram follows Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023).




The lecture, following a distinction inspired by human long-term memory, classifies memory by content — not by the underlying store:



Type
What it stores
Write / read, as the lecture frames them
A standard example




Episodic
Experience: what happened
Write an append-only event stream; read by a retrieval score
Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023)


Semantic
Knowledge: what is true, or believed
Write by reasoning over events; read by retrieval
A distilled fact or profile, not the raw log


Procedural
Skills: how to do a thing
Write as code-like skills; read by embedding retrieval
Voyager (Wang et al., 2023)



A useful test is: if you deleted the current prompt, what would still be there? The event log, the notes the agent wrote to itself, the skills it saved. That is memory. The tokens on the present screen are only the working set.


Tools, in brief
Tools are how the core reaches the environment. Early papers taught models to choose a tool, not only to talk about one. Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) trains a language model to decide which API to call, when, with what arguments, and how to put the result back into the text. The tools in that paper are a calculator, a question-answering system, a search engine, a translation system, and a calendar. Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023) focuses on calling a large number of APIs correctly.
The shape of a single call — select, fill arguments, validate, execute, return the result to context — belongs with compound AI systems, alongside RAG and MCP. The architectural point here is simpler: without tools, the agent can only speak; with tools, speech can become an action.


In one table







Piece
Role in the loop




LLM core
The model that writes thoughts, tool calls, and replies


Planning and reasoning
Intermediate generations that update the agent’s state before an act


Memory
Experience, knowledge, and skills that do not all fit in the current window


Tools
The actions: retrieval, code, search, files, and so on


Environment
What the agent observes and changes: OS, browser, repo, database, user


The loop
Observe, think, act, see what happened, repeat — as in ReAct





FAQ
Is this the same as a reinforcement-learning agent? Same loop, different flesh. Sutton and Barto’s agent observes, acts, and receives a next state and a reward. An LLM agent often has no scalar reward at each step: it has a thought, a tool result, and a user. The history page traces how one picture became the other.
Do I need several agents? Not to start with. A single loop with tools and memory is already an agent architecture. Multiple agents — debate, or an orchestrator and specialists — are a way to split work or to criticise a draft. They also add coordination failures, which is why they show up again under challenges.
Where does RAG sit in this diagram? Retrieval is a tool, and the retrieved text is context, which is a kind of memory. RAG is important enough, and standard enough, to have its own treatment on Compound AI systems and in the Lecture 3 pages starting at Why RAG.
What should I read first? Weng’s LLM Powered Autonomous Agents for a guided tour of planning, memory and tools; ReAct for the loop itself; CoALA for a more formal cognitive-architecture vocabulary.

History of agents
Compound AI systems
Key challenges in building agents

title: Compound AI systems
text:
Not just a model






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


A compound AI system is a system that uses a language model plus other components. Retrieval, tools, code execution, ranking, control flow written in ordinary software — all of that counts. The name, and the argument that leading results increasingly come from such systems rather than from a single monolithic model, is from Zaharia, Khattab, Chen, Davis, Miller, Potts, Zou, Carbin, Frankle, Rao and Ghodsi, The Shift from Models to Compound AI Systems (BAIR, 18 February 2024). CS 329Z Lecture 1 takes that essay as the frame for this part of the course.
The lecture also splits agent engineering into three layers, which is a useful map even before you choose a design:

the system — architecture, control flow, tools, interfaces;
the data — training examples, demonstrations, whatever you put in context;
the evals, and the metric they implement.

Most of this page is about the first layer. Data and evaluation come back under Key challenges.






Everyday example



A chef is not a recipe. A restaurant is a chef, a pantry, a set of utensils, a ticket rail that says which tickets come next, and a pass where someone checks the plate before it leaves. You can hire a better chef and still send out the wrong dish if the pantry is empty or the rail is a mess. A language model is the chef. RAG is the pantry. Tools are the utensils. The ticket rail is the control flow — and the interesting design question is who writes it: a person, in code, or the model, step by step.




Who decides the next step?
The lecture’s distinction is sharp, and it is about control, not about marketing.
Both a workflow and an agent can be compound AI systems. In a workflow, code fixes the steps. The model fills in a stage: it drafts, or scores, or classifies, but the graph is already drawn. The lecture’s examples are Agentless and AlphaCode 2: programmed pipelines that may sample and filter a lot of candidates, still under a fixed skeleton. In an agent, the model decides the steps. It looks at the current state and chooses a tool or a reply; the path is not wired in advance. The lecture’s example is SWE-agent.





flowchart TD
  subgraph workflow [Workflow]
    W1[Code already fixed the steps] --> W2[The model fills a stage] --> W3[The next coded step]
  end
  subgraph agentloop [Agent]
    A1[The model chooses the next step] --> A2[A tool call or a reply] --> A1
  end






This is not a moral ranking. A workflow can be more reliable precisely because the path is narrow. An agent can attempt tasks whose steps you could not have listed. Many production systems sit in between: a coded outer loop with a little agency inside a step, or an agent whose tools are themselves small workflows. The question to ask is always the same: who is allowed to decide what happens next?







Figure 1: Workflows versus agents: who decides the next step — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 56. The chart and the AlphaCode 2 example are from Zaharia et al., The Shift from Models to Compound AI Systems (BAIR, 18 February 2024).






Retrieval-augmented generation
RAG is the most familiar compound pattern. The model is connected to an external knowledge source at run time, so the answer can rest on documents the model was never trained on, and that you can inspect.
The lecture’s three steps are the usual ones:





flowchart LR
  Q[The question] --> R[1. Retrieve] --> A[2. Augment] --> G[3. Generate]







Retrieve — search your documents for passages that look relevant.
Augment — add those passages to the user’s question as context.
Generate — let the model write an answer that can use the retrieved facts.








Figure 2: Retrieve, augment, generate — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 57.




In the agent architecture, retrieval is a tool, and the retrieved text is context. The reason RAG gets its own heading is practical: it is how many systems first leave the frozen model. The fuller account — why retrieve, how the index is built, how a passage is scored, when retrieval becomes an action, and where the loop fails — is in the Lecture 3 pages starting at Why RAG.


Anatomy of a tool call
Tool use is the more general pattern. A model that can only retrieve documents is already useful. A model that can also read a file, run a test, or query an API can change the environment, not only quote it.
The lecture breaks one call into four stages:





flowchart LR
  S[Select] --> A[Arguments] --> V[Validate] --> E[Execute]
  E --> C[Result returns to context]







Select — which tool, from the schemas sitting in context.
Arguments — fill the typed fields from the task (a path, a query, a command).
Validate — check the arguments against the schema, sometimes with constrained decoding, before anything runs.
Execute — preferably in a sandbox; then return the result to the model’s context so the next thought can use it.

The lecture’s toy example is “What does test.py contain?”: the model selects a read_file tool, fills { "path": "test.py" }, the path is checked as a string, the file body comes back, and the model can now answer. The interesting engineering is all the cases that are not this simple: the wrong tool, a path that escapes a directory, an argument that looks well-typed and is still harmful, a result so large it drowns the next prompt.







Figure 3: The four stages of a tool call, with a read_file example — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 58.




Two papers that taught models to choose tools, rather than merely describe them, are discussed on the architectures page: Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) and Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023).


Model Context Protocol
Once you have many tools, and many data sources, the integration problem ceases to be a model problem and becomes a socket problem. Each new application should not need a one-off adapter to each new model host.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for that socket: a common way for a host (the application that owns the model) to connect to servers that offer tools, data, and other context. CS 329Z Lecture 1 points at the architecture page of the 28 July 2026 documentation. The idea to carry away is not a particular field in the spec. It is the move from “we wired this one API into this one agent” to “tools and context are interchangeable behind a protocol”.







Figure 4: MCP as a standard socket between applications and tools or data — CS 329Z Lecture 1 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 59. Diagram after the MCP architecture documentation (28 July 2026).






In one table







Idea
In one sentence




Compound AI system
An LLM plus other components, not a model alone (Zaharia et al., 2024)


Three layers
System, data, and evals — the job of engineering an agent


Workflow
Code fixes the steps; the model fills a stage


Agent
The model decides the next step


RAG
Retrieve, augment the prompt, then generate


Tool call
Select, fill arguments, validate, execute, return the result


MCP
A standard interface between a model host and tool or data servers





FAQ
Is every agent a compound AI system? In the sense of this lecture, yes, once it has tools, retrieval, or any control flow around the model. A lone completion from a frozen model is not. The converse is false: a RAG pipeline with a fixed retrieve-then-generate graph is a compound system, but it is a workflow, not yet an agent.
Why not let the model do everything? Because the model’s parameters are a poor place to store your latest documents, a poor calculator, and a poor permission system. Retrieval, tools, validation, and sandboxing exist for reasons a bigger model does not remove. The BAIR essay is explicit about this: some of the gains now come from engineering the system, not only from scaling training.
Is MCP a kind of agent? No. It is a protocol that agents (and other hosts) can use to reach tools and data. You can have agents without MCP, and MCP connections without much agency.
Where do evaluation and safety fit? They are the other two layers, and they are easy to postpone until a demo looks good. That postponement is itself a key challenge. Kapoor et al., AI Agents That Matter (arXiv, July 2024), is the reading for why accuracy-only agent benchmarks can mislead.

title: Why RAG
text:
A frozen typist, and a library next door






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


A language model only knows what it was trained on. Ask it something that changed last week, or that lives in your own files, and it will still try to answer — from memory, or from a plausible guess. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the simple alternative: look the fact up, put the passage in the prompt, and then write.
That idea is already named, briefly, on Compound AI systems and on the older RAG outline. This page is the reason to retrieve, and the shape of the loop. The next four pages take indexing, retrievers, agentic RAG, and failure modes.






Everyday example



You ask a colleague which office hour is quietest this week. If they answer from habit — “Wednesday afternoons are usually calm” — they may be wrong this week. If they glance at the queue log and then answer, you get a number you can check. The language model is the colleague. The log is the retriever. RAG is the habit of looking first.









Figure 1: Without retrieval the model guesses from habit; with a queue log it can cite this week’s numbers — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 10. The office-hour figures are a lecture illustration, not a measured dataset. Lecture original.






Why retrieve, rather than memorise?
The lecture’s list is short, and it is still the right list:

Just in time. You give the model the relevant passage when it is needed, instead of asking it to memorise the whole library.
Dynamic. Adding or updating a document is an index change, not a training run. That is how a system keeps up with a queue log, a policy wiki, or last quarter’s filing.
Interpretable. The model can point at the passages it used, so a person can check the answer.

Open-domain question answering was the early proving ground. Chen et al., 2017 (Reading Wikipedia to Answer Open-Domain Questions, DrQA) already split the job into a retriever, which picks passages from a large collection, and a reader, which writes the answer from those passages. The retriever in that paper was a fixed TF–IDF index; the reader was a neural reading-comprehension model. Today the reader is often a language model, but the split is the same.


The RAG loop
Lewis, Perez, Piktus and colleagues named the modern recipe retrieval-augmented generation. A query encoder looks up passages in a non-parametric document index (they use a dense retriever in the style of DPR); a generator — in the paper, an encoder–decoder such as BART — writes the answer given the query and the passages. The retriever and the generator can be trained together, by maximising the marginal likelihood of the answer. Related lines of work, which the lecture points to, include REALM and DPR.
The lecture credits this figure as Lewis et al., 2021. The paper appeared at NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv, May 2020). We follow the venue year here.







Figure 2: The RAG model: a retriever over a document index, a generator that writes from the query and the passages, and a training signal that can run through both — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 14. Original: Lewis et al. (2020). The lecture labels the paper 2021; it was published at NeurIPS 2020.




Formally, a retriever \(p(z \mid x)\) returns the top-\(K\) passages for a query \(x\), and a generator \(p(y \mid x, z)\) writes the answer one token at a time. The answer’s probability is approximated by a sum over those passages:
\[
p(y \mid x) \approx \sum_{z \in \mathrm{top\text{-}K}} p(z \mid x)\, p(y \mid x, z).
\]
The paper compares two ways to do the sum. RAG-Sequence picks a passage and sticks with it for the whole answer. RAG-Token may pick a different passage at each token. Most production pipelines today are closer to the first idea, or to a still simpler naive recipe: retrieve once, stuff the passages into the prompt, generate once. The jointly trained models in the paper are the research ancestor, not the only way to wire the loop.







Figure 3: A retriever over passages and a generator over query plus passage, with RAG-Sequence versus RAG-Token — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 16. The formulation follows Lewis et al. (2020). Lecture original.









flowchart TD
  Q["Query"] --> R["Retriever: top-K passages"]
  D["Document index"] --> R
  R --> A["Augment the prompt"]
  Q --> A
  A --> G["Generator writes the answer"]








Naive, advanced, and modular
Once you have retrieve-then-generate, people start adding steps around it. A survey by Gao, Xiong, Gao and colleagues (posted in December 2023, and usually cited as 2024) is the lecture’s map of those variants.

Naive RAG indexes, retrieves, and prompts a frozen model.
Advanced RAG adds work before and after retrieval: query rewriting, reranking, summarising, fusing passages.
Modular RAG treats those steps as interchangeable parts — rewrite, retrieve, rerank, read, even loop — so a system can be a pipeline or a small graph of skills.








Figure 4: Naive, advanced, and modular RAG, as mapped by the 2024 survey — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 21. Original: Gao et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey (2023/24).




The rest of this lecture is about making those parts honest: how you cut and index the library, how you score a passage, when retrieval itself becomes an action, and where the loop fails.


In one table







Idea
In one line

RAG-Sequence / RAG-Token

Naive / advanced / modular

FAQ
Is RAG the same thing as an agent? No. A fixed retrieve-then-generate graph is a workflow, and a compound system. It becomes more agent-like when the model decides whether to retrieve, what to ask, and when to stop. That is the subject of Agentic RAG. The distinction is the one already drawn on Compound AI systems.
Does retrieval replace fine-tuning? It replaces the need to bake every fact into the weights. You may still fine-tune for style, tools, or a domain. The point is that a document that changes tomorrow should not wait for a training run.
Why not put the whole library in the context window? Because longer is not always better — see context rot — and because a good index lets you pay only for the passages that matter. Retrieval is how you keep the window small and still reach a large store.
Where should I go next? Indexing is how the library is cut and stored. Retrievers are how a query finds a passage.

title: Retrievers for RAG
text:
Three ways to find a passage






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


Once the library is cut and shelved, a query still has to find a card. The lecture contrasts three families: word-overlap with BM25, a single vector per passage with DPR, and token-level late interaction with ColBERT. They fail differently, which is why people often run two of them and fuse the lists, then — if they can afford it — rerank a shortlist with a cross-encoder.






Everyday example



You are looking for a colleague’s desk. A door plate with their exact name is BM25: unmatched if you only remember a nickname. A receptionist who understands “the person who handles invoices” is a dense retriever: good on paraphrase, shaky on a typo in an error code. A late-interaction model is a receptionist who also glances at every word on the badge. A cross-encoder is walking over and having a full conversation with each candidate — accurate, and impossible at the scale of the whole building.




BM25
BM25 (Robertson and colleagues; the standard account is The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond, 2009) is still the default sparse retriever. Each query term contributes a weight that grows with how often it appears in the document, saturates so that the tenth occurrence counts for little, is damped if the document is long, and is scaled by an inverse-document-frequency term: rare words count more than words that appear everywhere.







Figure 1: The BM25 score: an IDF weight for each query term, a saturating term frequency, and a length normalisation — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 41. The formula is the usual BM25 implementation (Robertson and colleagues). Lecture original.




The IDF the lecture writes,
\[
\mathrm{IDF}(q_i) = \ln \frac{N - n(q_i) + 0.5}{n(q_i) + 0.5},
\]
is the common Lucene-style form, with a \(0.5\) smoother. Implementations differ in small ways; the idea does not: a term that almost every document contains should not dominate the score. BM25 still wins on exact literals — product IDs, error codes, names — and still misses paraphrase and synonyms.


DPR: dense passage retrieval
Dense Passage Retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020) is the lecture’s representative bi-encoder. Offline, a passage encoder \(E_P\) writes one vector per passage into an index. At query time a separate query encoder \(E_Q\) writes a query vector, and the system returns the passages with the highest inner product \(E_Q(q)^{\top} E_P(p)\), using maximum inner-product search. The two encoders are BERT-sized networks, trained with a contrastive loss, in-batch negatives, and BM25 hard negatives.







Figure 2: DPR’s bi-encoder: passages are encoded once into a vector index; a query is encoded at run time and scored by a dot product — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 43. The pipeline follows Karpukhin et al. (2020). Lecture original.




The paper reports that this dense retriever beats BM25 on four of five open-domain QA datasets, with SQuAD the usual exception — a collection where the questions were written against already-chosen paragraphs, so word overlap is an unusually strong baseline. The lecture shows the paper’s top-20 and top-100 table. Training on as little as a thousand question–answer pairs is, in that paper, already enough to beat BM25; the same work also reports end-to-end gains over earlier retrieve-and-read systems such as ORQA and REALM, without an extra pretraining stage. Those comparisons are Karpukhin et al.’s, not a rerun of our own.







Figure 3: Top-20 and top-100 retrieval accuracy: DPR beats BM25 on four of five datasets — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 47. Original: Table 2 of Karpukhin et al. (2020). SQuAD is the dataset where BM25 stays competitive.






How a retriever is scored
Before you believe a bake-off, you need a metric. The lecture’s short set, all averaged over queries, is worth keeping straight:

Hit@k is 1 if any relevant passage is in the top \(k\), else 0. Position inside the \(k\) does not matter. Failed@k is one minus that, and is the quantity Anthropic plots on the indexing page.
nDCG@k credits graded relevance and discounts by rank, then divides by the score of the ideal ranking.
MRR@k uses the rank of the first relevant passage (and counts 0 if it is missing from the top \(k\)).
Recall@k is the fraction of all relevant passages that made the top \(k\).

Hit tells you whether something useful appeared. Recall tells you how much of the useful set you found. nDCG and MRR care about order.


Hybrid search, then a reranker
The two cheap retrievers fail differently: BM25 misses paraphrase; dense retrieval misses rare literals. Hybrid search runs both and fuses the lists. Reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, 2009) merges positions rather than raw scores, so you do not have to calibrate two different scoring scales:
\[
\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + \mathrm{rank}_r(d)},
\]
with \(k = 60\) a common default. It works with any number of retrievers.
A cross-encoder then reranks a shortlist. The lecture cites Humeau et al. (2020) (Poly-encoders) for the contrast: a bi-encoder encodes the query and the passage separately, which is what lets you pre-compute an index; a cross-encoder reads them together, with full attention across both, and is accurate enough to score a few dozen candidates, not a corpus. You retrieve first, then rerank.


ColBERT: late interaction
ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, SIGIR 2020) sits between the two. Query and passage are still encoded independently, so the passage can be indexed offline. But you keep one vector per token, not one vector per document. At scoring time each query token takes a MaxSim — the best-matching passage token — and those scores are summed:
\[
S_{q,d} = \sum_{i \in q} \max_j \; \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{d}_j.
\]
That is late interaction: the expensive token-level meeting happens only at the end, and only against candidates you can afford.







Figure 4: ColBERT’s late interaction: a query encoder and a document encoder meet at MaxSim over token vectors — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 52. Original: Khattab and Zaharia (2020).




The cost is the index: you store tokens, not documents. The lecture’s latency table, from Khattab and Zaharia on MS MARCO, and with DPR’s “tens of milliseconds” taken from Karpukhin et al. on different hardware, is a qualitative map, not a single-benchmark bake-off.







Figure 5: A qualitative map of retrievers: what they pre-compute, how fast they are, and where they break — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 54. Latencies for BM25, ColBERT and the cross-encoder are from Khattab and Zaharia (2020), on MS MARCO; the DPR line is from Karpukhin et al. (2020), on different hardware.

  Q["Query"] --> B["BM25: exact terms"]
  Q --> D["DPR: one vector per passage"]
  Q --> C["ColBERT: one vector per token"]
  B --> F["Fuse ranks, e.g. RRF"]
  D --> F
  C --> F
  F --> X["Optional cross-encoder on a shortlist"]
  X --> K["Top passages into the generator"]

FAQ
If DPR beats BM25, why do people still run BM25? Because the wins are not the same wins. The papers the lecture cites still lose on some collections (SQuAD, in the DPR table), and BM25 is cheap, robust, and uniquely good at literals. Hybrid search is the usual peace treaty.
Is ColBERT “just a better DPR”? No. DPR collapses a passage into one vector before the query arrives. ColBERT keeps token vectors and lets the query meet them with MaxSim. That is more expressive, and more expensive to store.
Can I use a cross-encoder as my only retriever? Not at corpus scale. The lecture’s figure — on the order of ten seconds per thousand passages in the 2020 MS MARCO measurement — is why you retrieve first and rerank second.
What should I read next? When retrieval itself becomes a decision in a loop, go to Agentic RAG. For the ways a well-scored passage can still sink the answer, see failure modes.

title: Failure modes of RAG
text:
When the library misleads






Source



A reader’s guide to part of CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan and John Yang; Engineering AI Agents, Stanford, autumn 2026). The outline and the pointers come from that lecture; the wording on this page is ours. The course is also listed under Resources.


A tidy pipeline can still be wrong. The last slide of the lecture is a map of where it goes wrong: on the way into the index, in the way the model reads what it retrieved, and in the loop that decides the next step. This page stays with that map. It does not invent rates or incidents the lecture does not give.






Everyday example



A badly labelled filing cabinet, a reader who skims only the middle of a pile, and a researcher who never decides they have enough sources: those are the three columns. Retrieval-side failures are about what gets into the context. Reader-side failures are about what the model does with it. Loop-side failures are about how the process runs on.









Figure 1: Nine failure modes, in three columns: retrieval, reader, and loop — CS 329Z Lecture 3 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang), slide p. 63. Lecture original.






Retrieval-side

Recall ceiling. If the evidence never made the top-\(k\), the generator cannot use it. No amount of careful prompting recovers a passage the retriever missed. This is why indexing and retriever choices are not plumbing: they set a hard cap on what the system can get right.
Stale index. Documents change; embeddings and inverted indexes do not, unless you refresh them. The lecture’s wording is blunt: “embeddings not update.” A queue log from last term will send people to the wrong office hour.
Permission leak. A retriever that cannot see who is asking may return a passage the user is not allowed to read, and the generator will happily quote it. Access control belongs at retrieval time, not only at the front door of the app.



Reader-side

Lost in the middle. Even when the right passage is in the window, models often use the beginning and the end more reliably than the middle. The lecture tags this as position bias. The usual name in the literature is lost in the middle (Liu et al., 2023). It is one more reason not to stuff the window — a point already made under context rot.
Distraction. A similar but irrelevant passage can pull the answer off course. Hybrid search and a reranker exist in part to reduce this; they do not eliminate it.
Evidence conflict. Two sources, or a source and the model’s own prior, can disagree. A pipeline that always “uses the context” will not tell you which one it believed, unless you ask it to.



Loop-side
These matter most once retrieval is an action, as in Agentic RAG.

Compounding error. An early bad query, or an early misread, poisons the later turns. The transcript looks busy; the answer is still wrong.
No stopping rule. Without a clear condition for finishing, the agent can search forever, or stop too soon. Search-R1’s prompt has an explicit path to <answer>; many ad hoc loops do not.
Prompt injection. Retrieved text is still text in the context window. A malicious or simply over-eager document can steer the agent: ignore the user, follow these instructions instead. Treat retrieved content as untrusted input, not as a system prompt.

FAQ
If Hit@k is high, is the system safe? No. Hit@k only says a relevant passage appeared. The reader can still ignore it, a later turn can still drift, and a disallowed passage can still have been in the list.
Is “lost in the middle” a reason to retrieve fewer passages? It is a reason to retrieve well, and to think about order and length, not a reason to give up on retrieval. Indexing and reranking are how you keep the useful passage out of the slush.
Where does this meet evaluation? The retriever metrics on the retrievers page catch recall and rank. They do not catch injection, stale documents, or a loop with no stop. You need tests for those too. Key challenges in building agents is the wider discussion of evaluation and safety.
